docs.title: ArgonSDK Field Guide
docs.text:
A community field guide for modding Chivalry 2 with ArgonSDK — the unofficial Unreal Engine 4 project that mirrors Torn Banner's development environment.

New here? Start with the Introduction, then check the Requirements and pick a walkthrough from the Tutorials Overview.

docs.title: Introduction
docs.text:
ArgonSDK is an Unreal Engine 4 project specialized for creating modded content for Chivalry 2. It attempts to mimic the real development environment ("SDK") used by Torn Banner developers. Due to unofficial nature of this project, it inevitably has a set of limitations that will be discussed below.

This project is designed to function within the Chivalry 2 Unchained infrastructure, which offers a streamlined process for mod distribution and loading.

docs.title: What is an Asset?
docs.text:
Unreal Engine Wiki

Any piece of content in an Unreal Engine project is an Asset. You can think of Assets like building blocks that you use to create your game and application. Assets can be of many different types, such as Static Meshes, Materials, particle systems, and sound cues. Some Assets are created outside Unreal Engine (for example, in other 3D applications like Maya or 3ds Max). Other Assets, such as Blueprints, are created directly inside the engine.

docs.title: Asset Types
docs.text:

  • Raw Assets
  • Cooked Assets

docs.title: Chivalry 2 bot behavior guide
docs.text: This guide explains how the game's normal melee bots are assembled, how their behavior candidates are configured, how combat movement is controlled, and which parts can safely be tuned or reused.

docs.title: Start here
docs.text:
Read the visual TL;DR first.

Bots are best understood as several connected layers:

  1. Behavior sets provide groups of possible behaviors.
  2. Behaviors describe a possible choice, such as Slash, Block, Wait, or Shove.
  3. Considerations score how suitable that choice appears in the current situation.
  4. Actions turn a chosen behavior into requests, such as attack, block, wait, or movement intent.
  5. The native combat controller manages combat target, movement, facing, spacing, and combat state while the bot is fighting.

These layers are related, but they are not interchangeable. A bot can have behavior objects cached without evidence that it is selecting them, and a bot can visibly fight through its combat controller without proving which UtilityAI behavior started that fight.

The guide’s most important reading rule

Configured behavior is not necessarily selected behavior. A list of actions or event reactions tells us what the bot is equipped to consider; it does not, by itself, identify the winner of a live decision.

docs.text: If you want to understand… Read… Why bot behavior is not a single script How bots work How weights, inputs, and curves shape a choice Decision-making and scoring The equations behind score shaping and spacing Behavior and movement formulas How documented considerations change from 0 to 1 Curve explorer The exact BS_*, BC_*, AC_*, I_*, TG_*, and controller names Asset and function atlas What attacks, blocks, feints, and reactions request Combat actions and reactions How a bot approaches, faces, circles, and maintains range Movement and spacing What difficulty and tuning settings can safely change Tuning and difficulty Which conclusions are firm and which remain open Evidence and limitations

docs.title: Evidence labels
docs.text:
The guide labels material by what supports it:

Label Meaning Observed Directly seen on a live bot in documented conditions. Configured Present in an authored behavior, behavior set, or class configuration. Recovered Established from the game implementation and described here in player-facing terms. Unknown Not established by the available evidence.

The label tells you what a statement means. For example, an Observed spacing response says a controlled test changed spacing; a Configured attack entry says an authored behavior can request that attack. Neither statement alone proves a complete ordinary-match decision trace.

docs.title: Glossary
docs.text: Term Meaning Decision maker A component that owns behavior candidates and can evaluate decisions. Normal melee controllers have general and combat-focused decision-making surfaces. Behavior set A named collection of behavior classes. It is an inventory of candidates, not a fight script. Behavior One candidate activity, with a relative weight, considerations, one action, and sometimes a target generator. Consideration A condition that turns a world signal into a 0–1 influence on a behavior’s score. Input The sensor behind a consideration, such as distance, elapsed time, nearby allies, or a random value. Curve The mapping that turns a normalized input into a preference or penalty. Action The work requested when a behavior is selected, such as issuing an attack order or holding block. Target generator A source of candidate targets for a behavior. Normal melee combat behaviors instead use the controller’s existing combat target. Combat target The actor currently being fought by the combat controller. Native combat controller TBLAICombatController: the controller layer that owns combat mode, target, movement, spacing, facing, and attack state. Personality A configuration layer that can choose or override behavior-set and event-reaction settings. Event behavior A behavior candidate associated with a combat event such as an incoming attack or parry success.

docs.title: What this guide is and is not
docs.text: This guide avoids implementation-dump detail and speculative explanations. It also does not provide instructions for enabling UtilityAI on sparring bots.

docs.title: Melee bot combat — TL;DR
docs.text:
Summary

A melee bot has configured behavior choices such as Slash, Block, Wait, Feint, and Shove. Those choices can request combat work, while the combat controller owns the immediate fight: target, spacing, movement, facing, attacks, and defensive state.

docs.title: Two layers, not one traced fight
docs.text:
flowchart LR S[Authored melee behavior set] -->|Configured: contains| B[Slash · Block · WaitShove · Feint candidates] B -->|Configured: attaches| A[Action requests] T[Combat target and active combat mode] -->|Recovered: controller processes| N[Range · facing · movementattack and defense state]

Plaintext: the authored set contains candidates with actions they can request if selected. Separately, recovered controller code processes target and combat-mode state to handle movement and combat. No arrow joins these layers because an ordinary-match decision winner and its contribution to a particular visible fight have not been traced.

Layer Short version Target Normal melee combat needs a valid controller-side combat target. Behavior set A behavior set is an inventory of possible choices, not a fixed combo script. Scoring Weight, distance, cooldowns, nearby allies, randomness, and other considerations shape which candidate is attractive. Action A selected behavior can request attack, block, wait, dodge, or a movement intent. Combat controller The controller produces the visible approach, range control, facing, attack state, and defense.

docs.title: What a normal melee bot is configured to do
docs.text:
Attack pressure Defense Movement and position Event-associated options Slash, Overhead, Stab, Feint, Shove Block, Dodge, Riposte Approach target, hold a range, face target, lateral combat motion Responses to incoming attack, shove, parry success, damage, and guard-break opportunities

The normal combat inventory is BS_Combat_Melee_Normal_C. Its main behavior candidates are:

BC_Slash_C
BC_OverheadStab_C
BC_FeintAttack_C
BC_Block_C
BC_Wait_C
BC_Shove_C

The asset and function atlas explains these names and the related actions, inputs, target generators, event sets, and controller functions.

docs.title: Three rules that prevent wrong conclusions
docs.text:
A behavior set is an inventory

Seeing BC_Slash_C or BC_Block_C on a bot shows that it is available to consider. It does not prescribe a fixed order such as “slash, then block, then shove.”

Cached is not selected

A bot can hold cached behavior objects without evidence that its decision layer selected one of them. Visible combat is also not proof that a particular behavior caused it.

Native combat movement is its own layer

The combat controller can pursue, face, move around, and fight a target once combat is active. That movement layer is separate from proving a specific UtilityAI winner.

docs.title: What is safe to rely on
docs.text: Established in controlled use Not a reliable public control Engage a valid target through the controller in a controlled setup. Treating engagement as proof of a General behavior winner. Use controller-side close-range spacing controls. Public control of native lateral-motion strength, phase, or direction. Use waypoint/path-following for repeatable scripted routes. Treating a behavior-set write as an automatic rebuild of existing behavior objects. Read or tune an exact live behavior instance for controlled research. Assuming a weight change guarantees a visible winner.

docs.title: Asset and function atlas
docs.text:
This atlas connects the guide’s plain-language concepts to the concrete classes and assets used by the normal melee bot. Names are useful for browsing assets, inspecting a live bot, and recognizing what a behavior configuration refers to.

A name is not a runtime trace

Listing an asset or function proves that it is configured or documented in the bot’s available surface. It does not prove that a specific live fight selected that asset, dispatched an event set, or invoked a function.

docs.title: Naming scheme
docs.text:
Prefix Meaning BS_ Behavior Set — a collection of behavior candidates. B_ General-purpose behavior. BC_ Combat behavior. A_ General-purpose action. AC_ Combat action. I_ Consideration input — a world-state sensor. TG_ Target generator — a source of candidate actors or locations. _C The generated runtime class for a Blueprint asset.

The authored UtilityAI assets live under /Game/AI/Utility/ in game notation. In the local semantic catalog, the same root is written as AI/Utility/.

docs.title: Controller and decision-making surfaces
docs.text: Name Role Status and limitation Chiv2AIController_Utility_C The standard melee AI controller class used by documented normal bot spawns. Observed/Configured. Carries both general and combat decision-making surfaces plus the native combat controller. GeneralDecisionMakerComponent Holds broad world and engagement candidates. Observed. Its cache can be intentionally cleared by some helper-spawn workflows. CombatDecisionMakerComponent Holds close-combat candidates and event-associated behavior sets. Observed. It can cache normal combat behaviors even when active decision dispatch is not established. TBLAICombatController The native controller layer for target, combat state, movement, spacing, and attack control. Recovered/Observed. It can drive visible combat independently of proof of a UtilityAI winner.

docs.title: Core normal-melee behavior sets
docs.text:
Asset/class Role Contents or purpose BS_Combat_Melee_Normal_C The documented normal melee combat inventory. BC_Slash_C, BC_OverheadStab_C, BC_FeintAttack_C, BC_Block_C, BC_Wait_C, BC_Shove_C. BS_Combat_Melee_Dumb_C A simplified combat-set variant. Similar normal combat inventory without BC_FeintAttack_C. BS_MeleeFighter_C General combat-engagement behavior set. Includes entering combat, responding to damage, and escaping close danger. BS_General_C General-purpose behavior set. Includes revive, combat-zone safety, and objective movement candidates.

Observed: the _Normal set and six cached behaviors were present on sampled direct and owner-created bots. Configured: the authored Normal personality row names _Dumb. Unknown: the selector/application path reconciling those surfaces and the complete ordinary-match sequence that chooses a set and behavior.

BC_OverheadStab_C AC_Attack_C Request Overhead or Stab; considers attack cooldown and nearby teammates. docs.title: Combat actions
docs.text: Action Function in human terms Important configured detail AC_Attack_C Ask the controller to pursue an allowed attack. Requests attack-oriented spacing before its attack request. AC_FeintAttack_C Attack, then possibly request a feint during the appropriate phase. Has authored attack and feint lists. AC_Block_C Request a temporary parry hold. Used by certain event-associated defensive behaviors. AC_Riposte_C Request a riposte-style follow-up. Used by parry-success behavior options. A_EnterCombatWith_C Give an enemy target to the combat controller and request engagement. The documented bridge from general engagement behavior to combat-controller target/state. A_MoveTo_C Move toward a chosen target or location using path following. This is waypoint/path movement, not native combat strafe.

docs.title: Common consideration inputs
docs.text:
Input Reads Used by I_TimeSinceLastAttack Time since the controller’s last attack. Slash and Overhead/Stab cooldown shaping. I_TimeSinceLastDidBehavior Time since a configured behavior last ran. Block, Feint, and Shove cooldown shaping. I_Distance Distance to the current target. Close-range Block preference and event-defense conditions. I_InfluenceCurrent An influence value at the current point. Overhead/Stab’s nearby-teammate consideration. I_Random A random consideration value. Feint frequency shaping. These inputs feed curves and then behavior scoring. See decision-making and scoring and behavior and movement formulas.

docs.title: Combat-controller functions
docs.text:
These names identify supported controller-facing operations. They explain the control surface; they are not a generic instruction to force a normal bot’s decision loop.

Function Plain-language effect Important limit Engage Set a combat target and begin entering combat. Requires valid parameters and a valid target; it is not evidence of a General decision winner. Disengage Request leaving combat. Clears combat engagement rather than merely stopping one movement request. Attack Store and pursue an allowed attack order. Direct external invocation has a narrower validation history than native behavior-driven use. StrafeAndKeepDistance Store spacing and strafe intent. It is not a deterministic strafe command; active behavior paths can overwrite its values. HoldBlock Hold defensive input. Competes with other controller action requests and combat state. ReleaseBlock Remove the controller’s held-block request. Does not describe every possible block source. Dodge Request movement-direction dodge behavior. Depends on combat context and available dodge behavior.

docs.title: Where to use the names
docs.text:
• Browse /Game/AI/Utility/ to inspect the authored behavior, action, input, or target-generator configuration.
  • Read the guide pages first to understand what role a name plays.
  • Use the names to recognize a live inventory or asset reference.
  • Treat a live cache as evidence of configured availability, not proof of a selected winner.

For the evidence boundaries that apply to all entries, read Evidence and limitations.

docs.title: Combat actions and reactions
docs.text: Combat behaviors describe the bot’s available close-fight options. They do not directly describe a fixed combo. Each behavior can become more or less attractive based on its considerations, then an action requests an attack, defense, movement intent, or short delay from the combat controller.

docs.title: Normal melee combat options
docs.text:
Behavior Player-facing intent Action request Evidence boundary Slash Make a standard horizontal attack. Request Slash and attack-oriented spacing. Configured: allowed attack and action wiring. Overhead/Stab Use a higher-weight attack option that can choose overhead or stab. Request Overhead or Stab. Configured: allowed attacks and considerations. Feint attack Begin an attack and potentially turn it into a feint. Request an attack; on the appropriate windup path, request a feint. Configured: action sequence. Exact live frequency is unknown. Block Defend for a short time. Request and hold parry, then release it. Configured: action and hold duration. Wait Avoid committing to an immediate attack. Keep a spacing intent and finish after a short wait. Configured: fallback behavior and wait range. Shove Use a close pressure or response option. Request Shove. Configured: allowed attack and recent-block/cooldown concerns.

The normal combat set contains these as available candidates. A live combat state showing Slash or Parry is not, by itself, proof that the corresponding behavior won a decision.

docs.title: Attack actions
docs.text: An attack action provides the controller with an allowed attack list and an attack-oriented spacing request. The controller then checks the current combat situation and carries out a usable attack when its combat gate and weapon/range conditions allow it.

docs.title: Player-facing combat-state lifecycle
docs.text:
stateDiagram-v2 [*] --> Holding Holding --> Windup: attack becomes usable Windup --> Release: attack releases Release --> Recovery: attack completes Recovery --> Holding: next combat opportunity Windup --> Holding: feint or cancelled path Holding --> [*]: combat/action ends

Plaintext: an attack request can pass through holding, windup, release, and recovery. A feint or cancelled path can return to holding; action completion or leaving combat ends the current path. These are player-facing combat states, not a proof of which behavior candidate won.

For an ordinary attack behavior, the player-visible lifecycle is typically:

  1. the action requests an allowed attack;
  2. the controller pursues range and attack state;
  3. the pawn enters combat states such as holding, windup, release, and recovery;
  4. the action watches relevant state changes to decide when it can finish.

This is why an attack request is not identical to an instant swing. It is a request that passes through controller movement, weapon availability, combat state, and action completion rules.

docs.title: Feints
docs.text:
The feint behavior is configured to begin from an attack list and, during the relevant attack window, choose a different follow-up from a feint list. It expresses the feint through a second controller attack request rather than through a separate player-input recipe.

Configured: the behavior can request a feint. Unknown: its exact live selection frequency and timing distribution in an ordinary match.

docs.title: Block and defensive actions
docs.text:
The normal Block behavior requests the controller hold parry at a reaction-oriented priority, waits for its configured hold time, then revokes the request.

This is important because defensive behavior is more than a visual animation:

  • the controller tracks who requested the defensive input;
  • a hold can persist while the action is active;
  • releasing the action removes that request;
  • competing actions can still be governed by action-completion and interruption rules.

The configured normal melee Block behavior is a short proactive defensive option. Event-associated defense behaviors can use more urgent settings when a specific incoming-combat event is available.

docs.title: Event-associated reaction options
docs.text:
The combat decision-maker configuration has slots for event-associated behavior sets. These are best read as reaction inventories: they define options that may be considered when the corresponding event is handled.

flowchart LR E[Authored event slotincoming attack, shove, parry, damage] -->|Configured: points to| I[Reaction behavior set] I -->|Configured: contains| C[Reaction candidates]

Plaintext: an authored combat-event slot points to a reaction set containing candidate behaviors. The diagram does not connect a live event to evaluation or a visible response: event dispatch, selection, and execution in an ordinary fight remain Unknown.

Event category Documented configured options What it means Incoming attack Block incoming attack, dodge back, wait; some variants include Jab. The bot has defensive and counter-pressure candidates for an attack threat. Incoming shove Attack through shove, block incoming shove, dodge back from shove. The bot has authored shove-response candidates. Parry success Riposte, counter with shove, riposte with feint. The bot has authored post-parry pressure options. Damage caused Slash, overhead/stab, wait. The bot can continue ordinary attack or wait behavior after causing damage. Enemy guard-break or CC Wait and guard-break punishment. The bot has a configured punish opportunity. Several other slots No authored normal-melee set is established. Do not infer a special reaction merely from the slot name.

Configured reaction is not observed reaction

The listed behaviors establish what an event set contains. They do not establish that a live event dispatched the set, that the decision layer was active, or that any listed behavior won.

Variant sets

Some documented variants simplify the response inventory. For example, a simpler incoming-attack variant can omit Jab, and a simpler parry-success variant can omit the feint option. These differences describe authored capability, not a measured difficulty curve or event frequency.

docs.title: Riposte, dodge, and punish behaviors
docs.text:
These event-associated actions are more specialized than the normal six-behavior combat set:

  • Riposte is an authored post-parry attack option.
  • Dodge back is a defensive movement response with configured conditions that include a specific incoming-attack context and a close distance band.
  • Counter with shove is an urgent shove option after a parry-related opportunity.
  • Guard-break punishment is an urgent attack option configured for very close pressure.

They show that the bot has distinct authored responses for some combat opportunities. They do not yet give us a complete observed map from every player action to every bot response.

docs.title: What this controls, does not control, and leaves unknown
docs.text:
Category Summary Controls Authored actions can request attacks, feints, parry holds, waiting, dodges, and event-associated pressure or defense. Does not control by itself An allowed attack list or configured event set does not guarantee an immediate move, swing, block, or reaction. Unknown A complete live event-to-winner-to-visible-response trace for ordinary melee bots.

See Movement and spacing for the controller layer that can carry attack and defensive requests into position, facing, and combat state when the engagement gate is active.

docs.title: Curve explorer
docs.text: Considerations turn a normalized world value into a score from 0 to 1. The curve does not predict a complete behavior winner. It shows how one input helps or hurts one candidate before other considerations, active actions, and decision rules are applied.

docs.title: Curve families at a glance
docs.text:
Curve type Good mental model Linear A steady ramp up or down. Polynomial A ramp that can react early or only near an extreme. Logistic A soft threshold. Logit A very sharp central transition. Normal Prefer a middle band. Sine Repeat a rise and fall.

The exact equations are in behavior and movement formulas.

docs.title: Explore documented normal-melee considerations
docs.text:
Select an example and move the normalized-input slider. The graph and numbers use the documented range and curve parameters for that consideration.

Consideration

Consideration curve A graph of normalized input on the horizontal axis and curve score on the vertical axis. Normalized input: 0.00 Raw input Range Parameters Curve score

Interpretation:

This is one consideration, not the final decision

The displayed value is one curve output. A behavior can have several considerations, and those are combined with its base weight and runtime decision/action rules. The explorer therefore must not be read as an attack probability.

docs.text:

Block distance 0–375 units Polynomial: \(M=-1, K=10, C=0, B=1\) Close targets preserve a high score; distant targets are penalized sharply. docs.title: Decision-making and scoring
docs.text:
When a bot has more than one possible behavior, it does not simply choose the one with the largest named weight. Each behavior starts with a relative bias, then its considerations make it more or less suitable for the current situation.

The result is best understood as a ranking signal:

“Given this target and situation, how suitable is this behavior compared with the other available behaviors?”

It is not a published percentage chance, and it is not a promise that the behavior will visibly run.

docs.title: The decision vocabulary
docs.text: Part Role in a decision Behavior set A group of possible behaviors. Behavior One candidate, such as Slash, Block, Wait, or Shove. Weight The candidate’s starting relative bias. Consideration A test that changes suitability based on the present situation. Input The world signal a consideration reads. Curve The function that turns the input into a 0–1 influence. Action The request made if the behavior is selected. Target generator A way to produce candidate targets, when a behavior needs one.

docs.title: How one candidate moves through the system
docs.text:
flowchart LR I[World inputdistance, time, allies, blocks] --> N[Normalize to 0–1] N --> C[Curve score0–1] C --> K[Combine this considerationwith the candidate's others] W[Behavior weight] --> S[Candidate score] K --> S S --> R[Rank against eligible candidates] R --> A[Action selectedor active action remains] A -->|If invoked: requests| F[Combat controller state]

Plaintext: recovered scoring logic normalizes a world measurement, shapes it with a curve, and combines it with the candidate's other considerations. That result and the behavior's relative weight contribute to a candidate score. Decision and action-lifecycle rules may select a new action or preserve an active one; if invoked, an action can request controller state. This diagram does not show a measured winner or guarantee a visible combat result in an ordinary fight.

A curve is not a winner probability

The orange curve in the Curve explorer is one consideration's score, not the chance that its behavior will visibly run. Other considerations, competing candidates, and active-action rules still apply.

docs.title: What the normal combat behaviors are configured to consider
docs.text:
The normal melee combat set includes the following authored candidates:

Behavior Relative weight Main configured concerns Requested action Slash 1 Time since the last attack Request a slash attack. Overhead/Stab 2 Attack cooldown and nearby teammates Request overhead or stab. Feint attack 1 Randomness and time since the last feint behavior Request an attack followed by a possible feint. Block 1 Distance and time since the last block behavior Hold parry briefly. Wait 1 A constant low fallback score Maintain its configured spacing intent and wait. Shove 2 Recent enemy blocks and shove cooldown Request shove.

Configured: these are the normal melee behavior definitions. Unknown: which one wins in every ordinary-match combat situation.

How to read the table

A weight of 2 does not mean “twice as likely to happen.” The other conditions can reduce a candidate sharply, and the decision system also has active-action and interruption rules.

docs.title: Inputs are measurements, not decisions
docs.text:
An input reports a world value. The behavior decides how much to care about that value through its curve.

Input category Example reader question Distance “Is the current combat target close enough?” Time since last attack or behavior “Has this action cooled down enough?” Nearby allies “Would this attack be awkward around teammates?” Recent blocks “Has the opponent recently blocked enough that a shove is attractive?” Random value “Should this lower-frequency variation be considered now?” Constant “Should this behavior retain a small fallback value?”

The same input type can behave differently in two behaviors because each behavior can give it a different range and curve.

docs.title: Curves turn measurements into preference
docs.text:
Inputs are normalized to a 0–1 range and then transformed by curves. A curve can make a behavior:

  • steadily more attractive as a value rises;
  • steadily less attractive as a value rises;
  • almost unchanged until a threshold;
  • strongly responsive to small changes;
  • best in a middle band.

For example, a close-range defensive behavior can use a distance curve that scores well nearby and poorly far away. A cooldown can use a curve that holds a behavior back immediately after use, then allows it to recover.

The exact score-shaping formulas are in behavior and movement formulas. That page also explains why several considerations are combined as strong, softened multipliers rather than as a simple average.

docs.title: Compare documented examples
docs.text: The Curve explorer provides an interactive comparison of the documented Slash cooldown, Block distance, Block repeat timing, Wait fallback, Shove-pressure, and Feint-randomness considerations. Each uses its documented range and parameters; use it to compare one curve output at a time, not to predict a final winner.

docs.title: Target generation differs between general and combat behavior
docs.text:
Some behavior types need to find a target first. A general engagement behavior can search for an appropriate enemy or a movement behavior can search for a destination.

Normal melee combat behaviors are different: their target-generator field is empty. They are configured around the controller’s already-established combat target.

This gives combat decision-making a simple practical dependency:

  1. the controller needs a valid combat target;
  2. combat behaviors evaluate the situation relative to that target;
  3. a selected action requests combat work against that target.

If there is no valid target, a target-dependent candidate can be unsuitable even if its nominal weight is high.

docs.title: From eligible to selected to complete
docs.text:
These stages should not be collapsed into one:

Stage Meaning Present The behavior exists in a set or runtime cache. Eligible Its target/context and basic conditions allow it to be considered. Scored Its considerations have produced a candidate score. Selected The decision system has chosen it over alternatives. Active Its action is currently in progress. Complete or interrupted Its action has reported completion or has been replaced under the action rules.

Present is not selected

A live inventory can prove the first stage. It cannot, by itself, prove the later stages. This distinction is especially important for event behaviors, because a bot can cache the possible reactions without an observed event dispatch.

docs.title: Active actions and interruption
docs.text:
Actions are not necessarily instantaneous. Attack, block, wait, movement, and event-response actions can persist until a combat-state transition, a timer, or another completion condition says they are done.

The decision system has rules for whether an active action is ready to finish or may be interrupted. This means a newly attractive behavior does not always replace the current action immediately.

Recovered: an active matching action can be preserved, while a completed or interruptible action can be replaced by a new winner. Unknown: a complete public equation that combines all active-action, inertia, and target-switching effects into the final score for every ordinary fight.

docs.title: Worked conceptual example
docs.text:
Imagine a bot that is close to its combat target shortly after using block:

  1. The Block behavior’s distance input may favor blocking because the opponent is nearby.
  2. Its “time since block” input may still penalize it because the bot blocked recently.
  3. The combined score therefore may be lower than the distance alone suggests.
  4. Wait, Slash, or another candidate can remain competitive.
  5. Even if Block looks good, an existing active action may still be allowed to finish first.

This example explains the model. It does not claim a recorded bot must choose one particular result.

docs.title: What this controls, does not control, and leaves unknown
docs.text: Category Summary Controls Weights, input ranges, curves, and considerations shape the relative suitability of authored behavior candidates. Does not control by itself A behavior’s weight or a single favorable input does not guarantee its selection or immediate execution. Unknown The complete ordinary-match winner trace and one closed-form model for inertia, active actions, target switching, and all runtime decision cadence.

docs.title: Evidence and limitations
docs.text: The bot has several layers, and different evidence can establish different things. This page keeps the guide precise about what is known, what is configured, and what remains open.

docs.title: Evidence labels
docs.text: Label Meaning Observed Seen on a live bot under documented conditions. Configured Present in a behavior, set, action, or controller configuration. Recovered Established implementation behavior, described here in game-facing terms. Unknown Not established by the available evidence.

docs.title: Current model at a glance
docs.text: Topic What is established Important limit Normal combat inventory Normal melee bots can have Slash, Overhead/Stab, Feint, Block, Wait, and Shove candidates. Candidate presence does not identify the winner of a live decision. Behavior scoring Inputs are normalized and curved; behavior considerations combine into a score. The complete final winner model is not represented as one known public equation. Combat target and engagement A controller can establish a combat target, enter combat, and drive combat movement. Visible engagement does not prove a General behavior was the recorded cause. Native movement Native combat movement can approach, maintain range, face a target, and produce lateral motion. Public deterministic control of lateral direction and strength is not established. Spacing Close-pressure range is a verified controller-side spacing control in controlled tests. Some written fields and named intents can be reset or overridden by active behavior/action paths. Waypoint movement Path-following can make repeatable scripted rings and routes. It is not the same as native combat orbiting and tends to face movement direction. docs.title: A behavior cache is not an action log
docs.text:
Runtime behavior objects can be present because a decision maker materialized its configured sets. That gives useful information about available candidates and their parameters. It does not prove:

  • that the decision maker is actively evaluating them;
  • that a particular behavior was selected;
  • that its action is currently in progress;
  • that it caused the visible swing, block, or movement.

docs.title: Native combat is not proof of one specific UtilityAI winner
docs.text: A controller can visibly pursue a target, maintain spacing, face an opponent, attack, and cycle through combat states. That establishes the controller’s combat layer. It does not alone tell us whether a General behavior, Combat behavior, external setup, or another path caused the engagement.

docs.title: Authored reaction options are not a reaction replay
docs.text:
An incoming-attack set can contain block, dodge, wait, or jab options. A parry-success set can contain riposte and shove options. That tells us what the bot is configured to consider.

It does not establish:

  • that the event was received by the decision layer;
  • that the event set was evaluated;
  • which candidate scored highest;
  • whether an active action prevented an immediate replacement;
  • what reaction will happen in every fight.

docs.title: A controlled test is not every match
docs.text: Controlled tests are useful because they isolate a target, range, behavior weight, or movement condition. Ordinary matches add moving targets, teammates, objectives, attacks, hits, pathing, timing, and broader AI state. A controlled result should be read as evidence for the tested relationship, not as a complete model of all match behavior.

docs.title: Why some questions remain unknown
docs.text: Kind of gap Example Safe interpretation No suitable live observation No naturally active ordinary AI is available in the current world. Do not manufacture ordinary-match causality from a test spawn. No supported public control Runtime lateral variation affects combat movement but has no stable public tuning interface. Do not publish private or guessed controls as a recipe. Incomplete causal trace A configured event set exists, but a winner is not attributed during a live reaction. Describe it as an available reaction inventory, not a guaranteed response. Different layers overlap A controller fights while a behavior cache exists. Keep controller execution separate from decision selection.

docs.title: How to use the guide responsibly
docs.text:
Use the guide to answer one of these questions:

  • What can this bot consider? Read the behavior and asset pages.
  • Why might this candidate become more or less attractive? Read decision-making and formulas.
  • What produces target-facing combat movement? Read movement and spacing.
  • What settings are safe to tune? Read tuning and difficulty.
  • How certain is a claim? Return to this page and check its evidence label.

When a result matters for a new control system, validate it in the specific context where it will be used. The guide supplies a map of the known surfaces and their limits; it is not a substitute for measuring a new runtime behavior.

docs.title: Behavior and movement formulas
docs.text: This page explains the parts of bot behavior that can be expressed as equations without pretending that the entire decision system is a known mathematical model.

docs.title: Reading the formulas
docs.text:
The formulas below describe configured scoring and the verified portions of spacing selection. They do not prove that a behavior was evaluated, selected, or executed during a particular fight.

A score is not a recorded decision

A behavior can be configured with a weight and considerations while the decision loop is inactive, while another layer drives combat, or while another candidate wins. Treat the equations as an explanation of the authored scoring machinery, not a replay of every bot action.

docs.title: From a world value to a consideration score
docs.text:
An input reads a world value such as distance, elapsed time, or a nearby-team influence. Its configured range turns that value into a normalized quantity:

\[ x = \operatorname{clamp}\left( \frac{v-v_{\min}}{v_{\max}-v_{\min}}, 0, 1 \right) \]

Plaintext:

normalized = clamp((value - range_min) / (range_max - range_min), 0, 1)

Where:

Symbol Meaning \(v\) The value read from the game world. \(v_{\min}\), \(v_{\max}\) The configured meaningful range for that input. \(x\) A normalized value from 0 to 1.

The bot then maps \(x\) through a configured curve and clamps the result to a score from 0 to 1:

\[ c = \operatorname{clamp}\bigl(f(x; M,K,C,B), 0, 1\bigr) \]

Plaintext:

consideration_score = clamp(curve(normalized, M, K, C, B), 0, 1)

The common curve shapes are:

Curve Formula before final clamping Reader interpretation Linear \(M(x-C)+B\) A steady preference or penalty as the input rises. Polynomial \(M(x-C)^K+B\) A preference or penalty that can be gentle at first and steep later, or the reverse. Logistic \(\frac{M}{e^{-10K(x-C-0.5)}+1}+B\) A threshold-like S curve. Normal \(M e^{-30K(x-C-0.5)^2}+B\) A middle-band preference: not too low, not too high. Sine \(\frac{\sin((x-C)2\pi)M+1}{2}+B\) A periodic variation; uncommon in the documented melee behaviors.

M controls direction and strength, K controls shape or steepness, C moves the curve horizontally, and B supplies its base level. A positive M generally rewards larger inputs; a negative M generally penalizes them.

Other supported curve types

The underlying system also has Logit curves. They are part of the general scoring machinery, but they are not necessary to understand the documented normal melee examples. The technical research record contains the full curve catalog.

docs.title: Combining considerations into a behavior score
docs.text:
A behavior begins with a base value \(W\), derived from its relative weight and decision context. For \(n\) considerations, the known behavior scorer uses a compensation amount:

\[ a = 1-\frac{1}{n} \]

Each consideration score \(c_i\) contributes a softened multiplier:

\[ q_i = c_i \left(1+(1-c_i)a\right) \]

The resulting configured behavior score is:

\[ S = W\prod_{i=1}^{n} q_i \]

Plaintext:

compensation = 1 - 1 / number_of_considerations
adjusted_i = score_i * (1 + (1 - score_i) * compensation)
behavior_score = base_weight * product(adjusted_i)

This is not plain multiplication. A high consideration score changes little. A low score strongly reduces the behavior, but compensation makes the reduction less abrupt than multiplying the raw scores alone.

If there are no considerations, the behavior retains its base value. While scoring, a behavior can stop evaluating later considerations once the running result is already too low to matter.

docs.title: Example: a close-range block candidate
docs.text:
The normal melee block behavior has a distance consideration. In reader terms:

  1. Measure distance to the current combat target.
  2. Normalize that distance against the behavior's configured distance range.
  3. Curve it so close targets score well and distant targets score poorly.
  4. Multiply that result with the behavior's other condition(s) and its base weight.

This explains why a block candidate can become unattractive at range. It does not establish that the block action will win, because other candidates, active actions, and decision rules can still affect the outcome.

docs.title: What the formulas do not quantify
docs.text:
The equations above are evidence-backed for input normalization, curve evaluation, and the consideration combination step. They do not provide a complete probability model of combat:

  • A behavior weight is a relative bias, not a percentage chance.
  • Inertia and active-action modifiers exist, but their complete effect on final winner selection should not be represented as a known closed-form equation here.
  • The final decision process can preserve, interrupt, or replace an active action.
  • A configured behavior may never be evaluated in a particular live situation.

docs.title: A supportable spacing model
docs.text:
The native combat controller selects a spacing goal from the current combat context. In simplified form:

\[ d_{\text{requested}} = \begin{cases} d_{\text{attack}} & \text{when an active attack order supplies a usable attack distance} \\ d_{\text{facehug}} & \text{for the facehug intent} \\ d_{\text{own-range}} & \text{for the bot's own attack-range intent} \\ d_{\text{enemy-range}} & \text{for the outside-enemy-range intent} \\ d_{\text{standoff}} & \text{for the standoff intent} \end{cases} \]

The controller then applies a runtime engagement-distance variation:

\[ d_{\text{goal}} = d_{\text{requested}} \times \nu(t) \]

Plaintext:

goal_distance = selected_spacing_distance * runtime_variance(time)

The existence of the time-varying variance is established, but it is not a supported public tuning control and should not be assigned a made-up equation. The realized range also depends on navigation, target motion, combat state, and controller updates, so it should not be treated as identical to \(d_{\text{goal}}\).

docs.title: What this controls, does not control, and leaves unknown
docs.text: Category Summary Controls Configured inputs and curves shape a candidate's score; verified spacing settings can change the requested distance goal. Does not control by itself A single weight, curve, or strafe request does not guarantee a selected action or deterministic orbit. Unknown The complete closed-form winner-selection model, the public control of runtime strafe variance, and exact ordinary-match decision causality.

docs.title: Technical source boundary
docs.text: These equations are compiled from the preserved UtilityAI scoring documentation and the bot-behavior research record. The latter contains the technical implementation evidence; this page intentionally presents only the user-facing conclusion.

docs.title: How melee bots work
docs.text:
A Chivalry 2 melee bot is not driven by one monolithic “fight” script. It combines a decision layer that describes possible behaviors with a combat-controller layer that owns the immediate fight: target, movement, spacing, facing, and attack state.

This separation explains several otherwise confusing observations:

  • A bot can have a full inventory of combat behaviors without evidence that its decision maker is currently selecting any of them.
  • A bot can approach, circle, face an opponent, and attack through the combat controller even when its decision-maker activity is not established.
  • Changing a behavior configuration and changing a movement setting are different operations with different effects.

docs.title: The layers and the untraced handoff
docs.text:
flowchart TD B[General behavior set] -->|Configured: contains| G[Engagement candidates] C[Combat behavior set] -->|Configured: contains| D[Close-fight candidates] G -->|Configured: attaches| E[Action requests] D -->|Configured: attaches| E T[Controller target and combat mode] -->|Recovered: per-frame processing| F[Native combat controller] F -->|Recovered: controls| H[Movement · facing · spacingattack and defense state]

Plaintext: general and combat sets contain authored behavior candidates with action requests. If selected, an action can write a controller request; the diagram intentionally does not claim that selection happened in an ordinary match. Separately, recovered native code uses combat target and mode state to drive movement and combat. The observed bot cache and visible fight do not connect these two layers into one traced decision-to-action path.

In practical terms:

  1. The bot has a controller, a pawn, and world information such as nearby characters and combat state.
  2. General and combat decision-making surfaces can hold behavior candidates.
  3. A behavior combines a weight, considerations, an action, and sometimes a target generator.
  4. If a behavior is selected, its action requests something from the controller.
  5. The combat controller carries out combat movement and combat-state work while its combat gate is satisfied.

docs.title: Controller and pawn
docs.text:
The pawn is the visible character: it moves, animates, receives hits, and has a weapon and combat state. The controller is the AI-side object that holds decision-making components and combat-control state.

The controller’s important combat responsibilities include:

  • remembering the current combat target;
  • tracking whether it is out of combat, entering combat, or fighting;
  • choosing an intended spacing mode;
  • producing movement and target-facing behavior;
  • holding or releasing requests such as block;
  • retaining attack-order information while an attack is being pursued.

The controller is therefore the practical connection between “a behavior wants to attack” and “the character enters windup, releases a swing, recovers, or moves toward an opponent.”

docs.title: Two decision-making surfaces
docs.text:
Normal melee controllers expose two related decision-making surfaces:

Surface Main purpose Typical content General Broader world behavior and target engagement. Enter combat, respond to damage, revive, move around objectives, escape a local danger. Combat Choices while a combat target already exists. Slash, overhead/stab, feint, block, wait, shove, and event-specific reactions.

Configured/Recovered: a general engagement behavior has a target generator and an action that can validate an enemy and request controller engagement. The combat set contains close-fight candidates configured around the existing controller-side combat target. Unknown: whether that general behavior initiated a particular ordinary-match fight.

Combat behaviors do not normally generate their own targets

The documented normal melee combat behaviors use the controller’s current combat target. Their target-generator field is empty. General behaviors, by contrast, can use generators that look for suitable characters or locations.

docs.title: Behavior sets are inventories, not scripts
docs.text:
A behavior set is a named group of behavior classes. The normal melee combat set contains behaviors for common attacks, defense, waiting, feinting, and shoving.

That tells us the bot has those options available. It does not mean the bot must run them in a fixed sequence such as “slash, block, wait, shove.” Each behavior has its own conditions and relative weight.

At runtime, a decision maker can materialize behavior objects from a behavior set. Those objects retain their own action settings, considerations, timers, and recent-action bookkeeping.

Cached does not mean active

A behavior object can exist on a bot while the decision layer is inactive or while another layer is providing the visible combat behavior. Do not use a cache inventory as a fight replay.

docs.title: From behavior to action request
docs.text:
A behavior describes a candidate activity:

Part Question it answers Weight How strong is this candidate before its situation-specific conditions? Considerations Does distance, cooldown, nearby allies, a recent block, or another signal favor it now? Action What should happen if this candidate is selected? Target generator Which targets should the candidate consider, if it needs to generate targets?

For a normal combat attack, the action can request an allowed attack type and an attack-oriented spacing intent. For a block, the action can request holding parry for a configured duration. For a wait, the action can request a spacing intent and delay completion.

Read behavior and movement formulas for the known score-shaping math. The important practical point is that a high behavior weight alone is not a guaranteed action: other considerations, active actions, and decision rules still matter.

docs.title: From action request to visible fighting
docs.text:
An action can request combat work, but the native controller determines whether it can carry that work out in the current situation. In broad terms, combat movement requires a valid combat target and an active combat mode. With that gate satisfied, the controller can:

  • close distance or maintain a requested range;
  • face the combat target;
  • make lateral movement shaped by its runtime combat-movement settings;
  • pursue an attack order;
  • hold or release defensive input;
  • react to the pawn’s changing combat state.

The visible state machine is familiar to players: idle, holding, windup, release, recovery, and related interruption or hit states. An action can use those state changes to know whether it has finished.

docs.title: A typical engagement, with evidence boundaries
docs.text:
This is the supported conceptual path, not a claim that every ordinary-match encounter has been recorded from start to finish:

  1. A general behavior may identify an enemy candidate.
  2. Its engagement action can ask the combat controller to engage that actor.
  3. The controller records the combat target, enters an engagement state, and begins combat movement.
  4. Once close enough, the controller can enter active combat.
  5. Combat behaviors are the configured candidates for attack, block, wait, feint, shove, and event-associated reactions.
  6. A selected combat action can request an attack or defensive control.
  7. The controller and pawn carry that request through combat movement and combat-state transitions.

Observed: native combat movement and attacks can occur while decision-maker activity is not established. Configured: normal melee behavior sets contain the candidates described above. Unknown: a complete ordinary-match trace that attributes each visible action to a specific decision winner.

docs.title: What this controls, does not control, and leaves unknown
docs.text:
Category Summary Controls The controller owns immediate combat target, combat mode, spacing intent, movement, facing, attack state, and defensive requests. Does not control by itself Having a behavior set or cached behavior does not itself make the behavior run. Unknown The full ordinary-match causal chain from perception through every decision winner to every visible action has not been established.

Next: Decision-making and scoring explains how a behavior becomes more or less attractive, while Movement and spacing explains the controller's combat-target-dependent movement.

docs.title: Movement, spacing, facing, and combat state
docs.text: The combat controller, not a behavior set alone, makes a melee bot physically approach, face, orbit, and fight an opponent. A behavior or action can request an intent such as “attack at my range” or “wait at standoff range,” but the controller turns that intent into movement only while it has a valid combat target and is in a combat mode.

docs.title: Entering and leaving combat
docs.text:
Recovered: a valid engagement request sets up controller-side target and mode state. When the combat gate is active, native per-frame processing can approach, face, and adjust position around the target. An immediate disengagement tears down that state.

This describes a controller capability, not an observed General UtilityAI behavior winning and causing engagement in every ordinary fight.

The controller-side target is the anchor for normal melee combat behavior. The documented normal combat behaviors do not independently search for targets.

flowchart LR E[Valid engagement request] -->|Recovered: sets up| T[Combat target and mode] T -->|Recovered: active gate| N[Per-frame native combat movement] T -->|Recovered: immediate Disengage| O[Engagement torn down]

Plaintext: a valid controller engagement request sets up a target and combat mode. When the combat target is present and the mode is not OutOfCombat, recovered per-frame code can handle combat movement. An immediate Disengage clears that engagement. The diagram does not establish the ordinary-match caller of Engage or every internal mode transition.

docs.title: Spacing intents
docs.text:
Combat actions can ask for a named distance intent:

Intent Human meaning Facehug Move into very close pressure range. My attack range Prefer the bot’s own usable attack range. Outside enemy attack range Prefer distance outside the opponent’s usable range. Standoff range Maintain a more neutral separation.

When no active attack order takes precedence, the controller selects a requested distance from the intent. An active attack order can instead supply an attack distance.

The supported conceptual model is:

\[ d_{\text{goal}} = d_{\text{selected intent}} \times \nu(t) \]

Here \(d_{\text{selected intent}}\) is the chosen range, and \(\nu(t)\) is a runtime engagement-variation factor. The controller then moves in response to the difference between the current and desired range.

Plaintext:

goal distance = selected spacing distance × runtime variation

The variation is intentionally left symbolic. It is known to affect runtime motion, but it is not a supported public tuning control with a documented stable equation.

docs.title: A verified spacing control
docs.text:
The facehug range is a verified controller-side spacing control in controlled movement-only tests. Changing it changed the realized approach distance while the target was stationary and offensive behavior candidates were suppressed.

That is an important distinction:

  • Facehug range: demonstrated effect on approach distance in the controlled setup.
  • Combat-target desired-distance field: persisted when written in testing, but did not provide a clear realized stand-off-distance effect by itself.
  • Named desired-distance/strafe requests: can be reset by active behavior/action paths rather than remain a durable manual movement command.

docs.title: Facing and lateral movement
docs.text:
While the controller is in combat, it can face the combat target closely while moving around it. Controlled observations show substantial lateral motion with target-facing yaw, including changes of orbit direction.

However, the named “desired strafing” request is not a deterministic circle-strafe API. The documented combat-movement implementation does not use that request as the direct source of lateral movement. Instead, private runtime variation settings influence strafe pattern, timing, and strength.

Do not promise deterministic native circling

A bot can visibly orbit and shuffle around a target, but the supported public controller surface does not expose a stable, repeatable direction/strength control for that motion.

docs.title: Native combat movement versus waypoint movement
docs.text:
There are two useful but distinct movement systems:

System Good for Main limitation Native combat movement Target-facing approach, close combat range control, and organic lateral movement while engaged. Lateral variance is not publicly deterministic. Waypoint/path-following movement Repeatable routes, exact rings, and scripted circles through chosen locations. The pawn tends to face the waypoint/movement heading rather than continuously face the opponent.

Do not combine both systems as though they were one steering algorithm. A combat controller and a path-following controller can compete for movement and facing ownership.

flowchart TB T[Combat target] --> N[Native combat controller] N --> NF[Target-facing, spacing,organic lateral movement] W[Waypoint route] --> P[Path-following controller] P --> PH[Route-facing, repeatablelocations and rings] N -. competing movement/facing ownership .- P

Plaintext: native combat movement owns target-facing engagement and variable combat motion. Waypoint movement owns a planned route. Use one as the primary owner when repeatability matters; running both as if they were one steering system can make movement and facing fight each other.

docs.title: What has been effective, unreliable, or unavailable
docs.text: Status Control or observation Interpretation Works in controlled tests Engage a valid target and use the combat controller’s native movement gate. Enables native approach, facing, and combat movement without proving a UtilityAI winner. Works in controlled tests Change the facehug range. Changes close-range approach distance under the documented test conditions. Works for scripted routes Use waypoint movement around a ring of locations. Gives repeatable circles, but it is waypoint steering rather than native combat strafe. Unreliable as a manual command Write desired distance or desired strafe mode while behaviors are active. Active action paths can replace those values. Not a supported public tuning control Runtime strafe pattern, direction, rate, and strength. They affect motion but are not exposed as a stable public interface. Unknown A deterministic native combat circle with independently chosen direction and strength. Requires a supported control surface or additional research.

docs.text: Category Summary Controls Combat target, combat mode, native approach, supported range selection, target-facing, attack-state movement, and defensive movement context. Does not control by itself A desired-strafe request does not command a stable clockwise/counter-clockwise orbit; a desired-distance write is not necessarily the active range goal. Unknown A public deterministic control for native strafe variance and a complete ordinary-match explanation for every movement adjustment.

docs.title: Personality, difficulty, and safe tuning
docs.text:
Bot difficulty is not one slider. It is expressed through a combination of behavior-set choices, event-response choices, personality values, controller movement variation, and the behavior objects already materialized on a bot.

The most useful tuning rule is simple:

Change the layer that actually owns the behavior you want to change, and verify whether the bot has already cached its runtime objects.

docs.title: Normal and simplified combat inventories
docs.text:
The documented normal melee combat inventory is BS_Combat_Melee_Normal_C:

Behavior What it adds BC_Slash_C Standard Slash option. BC_OverheadStab_C Overhead or Stab option. BC_FeintAttack_C Feint-capable attack option. BC_Block_C Brief defensive parry option. BC_Wait_C Low-score wait and spacing option. BC_Shove_C Shove pressure option.

The documented simplified variant, BS_Combat_Melee_Dumb_C, removes the feint behavior. Event sets also have simpler variants; for example, a simplified incoming-attack set can omit Jab and a simplified parry-success set can omit the feint follow-up.

This is a useful configured capability difference. It is not, by itself, a complete measured difficulty curve.

docs.title: What was observed on sampled bots
docs.text:
Observed: documented direct test spawns and an owner-created bot had the normal combat set and all six normal combat behaviors, including BC_FeintAttack_C, in their caches. This establishes what those sampled bots held, not the selection rule for every default or ordinary-match bot.

Configured: the Normal personality row names the simplified _Dumb melee set. The difference from the sampled _Normal caches could reflect the spawn path, row application, or another configuration choice; it has not been reconciled. The general runtime selector and reapplication path for personality rows remain Unknown.

Question Supported answer What did the sampled direct/owner-created bots hold? Observed: the six-candidate _Normal cache, including Feint. What does the authored Normal personality row name? Configured: the simplified _Dumb set. This is not a record of what a sampled bot received. Can the authored data contain simplified and advanced variants? Configured: yes. Is there a universal public call to choose any personality row for each newly spawned bot? Unknown: not established. Does changing a shared controller default automatically change an existing spawn? Observed: no reliable propagation was demonstrated.

docs.title: Behavior sets versus runtime behavior caches
docs.text:
Behavior sets are class-level inventories. A decision maker can create runtime behavior objects from them, and those objects retain their own weight, action, consideration, and timer state.

flowchart LR S[Authored behavior setBS_Combat_Melee_Normal_C] -->|materializes| C[Runtime behavior cache] C --> I[Live behavior instancesweight, timer, action state] SR[Change set reference] -. does not by itself rebuild .-> C IW[Change live instance weight] --> I

Plaintext: the authored set can be used to create cached runtime objects, which in turn contain the live behavior instances. Changing a set reference changes that reference; it does not itself rebuild the existing cache. Changing an instance's weight reaches that instance, but does not guarantee that a decision loop evaluates it, that it wins, or that it becomes visible.

This produces an important cache boundary:

Change What it changes reliably What it does not guarantee Change a behavior-set reference The configured set reference. Rebuilding an already-existing behavior cache. Change a live behavior instance’s weight That instance’s relative scoring bias. A selected winner, active decision loop, or a complete ordinary-match result. Change an event-set reference The configured reaction-set reference. Replacing a cached event behavior array immediately. Change a shared class default The shared default object. Propagation into existing separately created instances.

Do not assume a set write rebuilds a bot

A live bot can retain behavior objects that were created before a behavior-set reference changed. Treat set replacement and runtime-cache rebuilding as separate operations.

Research-only movement isolation

In controlled research, attack pressure was reduced by changing live weights on the offensive normal-combat behavior instances: BC_OverheadStab_C, BC_Shove_C, BC_FeintAttack_C, and BC_Slash_C. This helped isolate native movement while the combat target and controller gate remained in place.

This is not a difficulty or UtilityAI-enabling recipe. Other behaviors may remain; changed weights do not prove that a decision maker ran, and changing live instances is different from replacing a behavior set.

docs.title: Personality and variance
docs.text:
Personality configuration can supply behavior-set and event-set choices and can influence combat variation. Some controller-side movement variation is initialized during possession and affects engagement distance and lateral movement.

The important practical limit is that the documented runtime movement variation is not exposed as a stable public tuning interface. A behavior or controller intent can request a spacing mode, but it does not provide a reliable public knob for exact lateral direction, rate, or strength.

See movement and spacing for the supported movement controls and their limits.

docs.title: Safe tuning checklist
docs.text:
Before calling a result a successful tuning change:

  1. Identify the owner: behavior instance, behavior-set reference, event-set reference, controller range, or movement path.
  2. Read back the changed value from the exact live object.
  3. Check whether the bot already has cached behavior objects.
  4. Measure the intended visible outcome separately from the value write.
  5. Restore or destroy only the test actor used for the experiment.

Unknown A universal personality-row selector/reapplication method and a complete public deterministic control for combat-movement variance.

docs.title: Chivalry 2 spawning guide
docs.text: This guide explains how the game brings players and bots into a match: which actors place and order spawns, how a spawn wave collects players, how queue policies affect timing, and which parts are authored map setup rather than live behavior. It describes the ordinary player-spawn system, not generic actor placement or what a character does after spawning.

docs.title: Start here
docs.text:
Read the visual overview first.

Inferred — working mental model: spawning is best understood as five connected layers:

  1. Spawn sequences order waves across a set of spawners and control how many can be active.
  2. Spawners create and configure a wave at a placed location.
  3. Spawn waves hold joining controllers, expose state, and release their spawner when they end.
  4. Queue policies decide who is admitted and how respawn timing is accumulated.
  5. Authored spawner Blueprints add camera, HUD, run-in movement, and control-restriction presentation on top of the native actors.

This five-layer picture is Inferred: the individual handoffs are recovered below, but complete mode ownership and dispatch are not fully traced. The layers are related but not interchangeable. A sequence object can exist without being active, a spawner can be placed without being selected, and a wave can hold membership that a particular callable did not write.

The guide's most important reading rule

Configured spawning is not the same as dispatched spawning. A placed sequence, a queuer instance observed under a mode object, or a callable method in the implementation tells us what the game is equipped to do. It does not, by itself, identify the path that produced a particular live spawn.

docs.text: If you want to understand… Read… The smallest correct mental model, with a diagram Spawn System Overview How the layers connect and where each handoff is established How spawning works What each sequence, spawner, wave, and queuer owns Components How wave, cumulative, and group queues differ Queues and timing What FFA, TDM, LTS, and TO configure and what was observed Game modes What to inspect in an existing map Map-reading guide Which spawner variants are named in authored assets Spawner types Where each spawner variant is placed and what it configures Spawner variants Which conclusions are firm and which remain open Evidence and limitations

docs.title: Evidence labels
docs.text:
The guide labels material by what supports it:

Label Meaning Observed Directly seen in a documented live match or controlled test. Configured Present in an authored level, class, or default configuration. Declared A native header exposes a class relationship, field, or callable surface; this alone does not establish what its body does. Recovered Established from the game implementation, described here in player-facing terms. Inferred A working explanation supported by evidence but not fully traced. Unknown Not established by the available evidence.

Labels belong to individual claims. For example, a Configured faction sequence says a map author set one up; it does not prove that an ordinary respawn used it. A Recovered call body says the implementation can do something; it does not prove that call ran in a given match.

Glossary Term Meaning Spawn sequence An actor that orders waves across spawners and limits how many run at once. Spawner An actor that creates and configures a spawn wave at a placed location. Forward spawn An authored forward-spawning call appears in Team Objective stage scripts. Its concrete receiver in the sampled map and its ordinary-match behavior remain Unknown. Spawn wave A temporary actor that collects joining controllers and tracks spawn timing and state. Wave state The wave's progression label, such as not started, spawning, or ending. Queuer A policy layer that admits controllers and schedules when they can spawn. It appears under a mode in samples; mode ownership is Inferred, not observed creation. Group spawner A spawner that aggregates child spawners and a selection mode. Run-in spawner An authored spawner variant with movement and presentation behavior for entering play. Control restriction A wave flag governing whether player control is limited during the spawn. Admission Adding a controller to a wave or queue; distinct from creating the pawn. Scope and reading limits

This guide keeps named surfaces where they help readers, but it avoids raw implementation dumps, speculative call chains, and instructions for authoring a new spawn system. Where the mechanism that produced a live spawn is not established, the guide says so instead of filling the gap with the most plausible story.

docs.title: Spawn System Overview
docs.text:
The smallest correct model — Inferred

A spawn sequence orders waves across placed spawners. A spawner creates a spawn wave, the wave collects joining controllers, and a queuer can govern who is admitted and when. Authored spawner Blueprints add the camera, HUD, and run-in presentation around that core. The exact native path that admits a player in an ordinary respawn is not fully established.

flowchart LR S[Spawn sequence] -->|Recovered: selects| SP[Eligible spawner] SP -->|Recovered: creates and configures| W[Spawn wave] C[Controller] -->|Recovered: can join| W Q[Queuer policy] -.->|Inferred: admission and timing| C W -->|Recovered: conditional end releases| R[Spawner releasedand cleanup scheduled]

Plaintext: recovered code shows a sequence selecting a spawner, the spawner creating a wave, and a controller being able to join that wave. A queuer can be the admission and timing policy, but its mode ownership and live dispatch are not fully traced. When its recovered end conditions apply, a wave releases its spawner and schedules cleanup. The complete ownership model is Inferred.

Layer Short version Sequence Orders waves, tracks active waves, and limits concurrency. Spawner Creates and configures a wave at a placed location. Wave Holds joining controllers, state, and timing; releases its spawner when it ends. Queuer A separate policy for admission and respawn timing; its ownership by a mode is Inferred from where it appears. Authored spawner Adds presentation and movement behavior on top of the native spawner.

For the full guide, return to the spawning guide landing page.

Sample and interpretation cautions

A separate observed sequence

In the TDM Wardenglade / InProgress sample, a player was without a pawn, then a faction wave had one joined controller, then a new pawn was possessed. Those are time-ordered observations, not an attributed controller-to-pawn call chain: the function that wrote the membership and created the pawn remains Unknown for that sample.

A placed spawner is an inventory entry

A spawner type being present in authored assets tells us it exists and what it can do. It does not say which spawner a live spawn selected.

A wave object is not a membership log

An empty wave in one snapshot can later hold a controller. A single sample does not establish what admitted that controller or which callable performed the spawn.

Missing calls at one entry point are sample-bounded

In the TDM Wardenglade / InProgress respawn sample, several spawn-related callables were not dispatched while a control callable did fire. That is a useful negative result for those entry points, not a complete model of every respawn path.

docs.text:
This page answers a narrower question than Spawner types: which authored spawner classes are actually placed in maps, and what configuration do they expose? The counts below are Configured typed actor exports in the indexed map data; “maps” counts map assets containing that type. They are not spawn counts, unique physical locations, or records of which spawner a live match selected.

Placement is not selection

A typed map export proves that a class was authored into a level. It does not prove that a sequence chose it, that a wave started there, or that it produced an observed player spawn.

docs.title: Falmire
docs.text:
Falmire is the clearest example of several variants appearing in one map family:

  • CagedSpawner_C is placed in FFA, LTS, TDM, and Team Objective Falmire.
  • BP_FreeableVIPSpawner_C is placed in Team Objective Falmire at the VIP spawn. Its authored wave parameters specify WarHeroSpawn_C and a private-wave flag; live use was not observed.
  • GroupSpawner is also placed in Team Objective Falmire.

These are authored placements. They do not show which caged, group, or VIP spawner was selected for a particular death or objective stage.

docs.title: Tournament Grounds
docs.text:
Across the indexed Tournament Grounds map variants, authored placements include FenceSpawner_C and all three Run-In subtypes:

  • RunInSpawner_Long_TG_C
  • RunInSpawner_Medium_C
  • RunInSpawner_Short_C

The subtypes differ mainly in camera offset and spawn-gate configuration, not in a demonstrated runtime rule.

docs.title: Configuration highlights
docs.text:
Base and authored presentation
  • BaseSpawner_C: spawn name “Main Force”, fade time 0.4, start-camera offset, vulnerable time 1.75, and a player-kill stage action.
  • BaseSpawner_C also carries camera fade, HUD marker, possession hooks, and cleanup of constructables and horses.
  • These are authored defaults; they are not evidence that a particular spawn used them.
Caged and Fence spawners
  • CagedSpawner_C: cage actor and state, caged-character list, exit point and key, eject velocity, and a two-second free delay. It permits invalid spawn locations and skips pawn overlap checks.
  • FenceSpawner_C: FenceSpawn animation, one player per wave, three-second pre-spawn, two-second vulnerability delay, and skipped location validation.
Movement and special-case variants
  • MovingBaseSpawner_C: attach-on-spawn enabled, replication enabled, and a relative-location map for waiting entries.
  • BP_FreeableVIPSpawner_C: Iron Maiden spawn animation, fade time 0.5, one player per wave, three-second pre-spawn, and a two-second vulnerability delay.
  • TutorialSpawner_C: no child-specific properties or functions were surfaced in the indexed data.
Run-In family
  • RunInSpawner_C: spline and autorun settings, a three-second stop delay, sprint movement, follow-first-spawned behavior, and wave sound overrides.
  • RunInSpawner_Long_TG_C: spawn-gate array, replicated start state, two-second pre-spawn, and a higher camera offset.
  • RunInSpawner_Medium_C: two-second pre-spawn and a middle camera offset.
  • RunInSpawner_Short_C: two-second pre-spawn, a shorter camera offset, and a slight downward rotation.

docs.title: What remains unknown
docs.text:
Runtime selection is not established

The indexed data tells us where classes are placed and how they are configured. It does not identify which class served an observed spawn, how a group spawner selected a child, or whether a Run-In path ran in an ordinary match.

For the ownership model around these actors, see How spawning works. For the component responsibilities, see Components. For the evidence labels used across the guide, see Evidence and limitations.

docs.title: Spawner types
docs.text: Spawners are actors that can start spawn waves at placed locations. The native ASpawner contract and the authored BaseSpawner_C Blueprint branch expose related surfaces; do not mistake their names for a fully verified compiled-class ancestry. The list below is an authored inventory, not a record of which spawner a live match selected.

How to read evidence labels
  • Recovered describes implementation behavior established from the game code and written in player-facing terms. It does not claim that a call ran in a particular match.
  • Configured describes something authored into a level, class, or default. It is an inventory of what is available, not a record of what was selected.
  • Observed describes a bounded live sample. Keep the map and match state in mind when reading it.
  • Unknown marks a genuine gap. It is not a hint about the most likely answer.

docs.title: Ownership versus presentation
docs.text:
Recovered native actors expose selection, wave creation, membership bookkeeping, and release operations; the function that wrote membership in the observed respawn is still Unknown. The authored spawner Blueprints sit around that core and provide what the player sees during a spawn — camera work, HUD state, movement along an authored path, and checks of the wave's control restriction.

Why the split matters

Seeing camera or run-in behavior does not prove which native spawner was selected, and seeing a wave with membership does not prove which authored presentation path ran. Keep the two layers separate when interpreting a match.
