docs.title: Spawning by game mode
docs.text:
Modes differ in what their level scripts author and in what live samples show. This page keeps those two things separate: a configured sequence is not a confirmed respawn path, and one live sample is not a rule for a whole mode.

Mode Configured Observed Unknown FFA Level scripts author a sequence reference and an activation call; maps expose different scoring and distance settings. FFA Fighting Pit / InProgress had a single active looping sequence with one spawner and one empty wave with a short pre-spawn delay. Whether that configuration is the ordinary player-respawn path; full actor and sequence inventories. TDM Separate faction sequences; Courtyard authors group-spawner references and Wardenglade authors named faction spawner references. Maps differ in simultaneous waves and interval length, with loop and fast-first-spawn flags. TDM Courtyard / InProgress samples alternated between no live sequences and active faction sequences; a queuer instance under the mode object and faction-paired empty waves were present. TDM Wardenglade / InProgress showed a wave gaining one joined controller and then a new pawn. Queue selection, which callable wrote membership, and whether the observed path holds on other maps. LTS Round and life settings on the mode; level scripts expose initial-spawner names and match-state presentation. LTS Courtyard / WaitingToStart had two inactive faction sequences and a queuer but no waves. Whether LTS bypasses, constrains, or uses the shared sequence/spawner/wave path, and when sequences activate. TO Stage scripts reference faction spawners, run-in spawners, sequence activation, and forward spawning. No ordinary-match forward spawn was established. Which concrete spawner the sampled stage event selects, and whether forward spawns occur in ordinary play.

docs.title: If you're inspecting a map
docs.text:
Use the mode comparison above as a reading guide, not as a tested recipe for creating a new spawn system:

  1. Find the authored level-script references and activation calls, then check whether the map names faction sequences, stage-specific spawners, or both. Their presence is Configured, not evidence that they were selected.
  2. Compare the sequence's authored loop, wave-concurrency and timing settings with its placed spawner types in Spawner variants. A typed placement does not identify which location served a player.
  3. In a live match, record the map, mode and match state before interpreting sequences or waves. A WaitingToStart LTS snapshot without waves is not evidence about its later rounds, and a TDM wave with membership does not identify the native join caller.

For an editor walkthrough that does construct a simple map, see the Free-for-All map tutorial. It is a separate tutorial, not proof that the sampled shipped maps use the same setup or that this guide has verified a new-map spawning recipe.

FFA details

Configured. Small FFA maps each author a level-script spawn-sequence reference and an activation call. Visible defaults differ: one map uses an FFA scoring method with a minimum-distance setting and penalty, another exposes larger minimum-distance values, and a third excerpt does not show equivalent numbers. Catalog truncation prevents a complete actor inventory.

Observed. In FFA Fighting Pit / InProgress, a single active looping sequence had one configured spawner and one empty, non-control-restricted wave with a short pre-spawn delay. No joined or queued player was present, so this does not establish an ordinary respawn path.

TDM details

Configured. Courtyard and Wardenglade author separate Agatha and Mason sequence construction and initialization paths:

Map Authored spawner references Simultaneous waves Seconds between waves Other visible flags Courtyard One named group-spawner reference per faction sequence 2 7.5 s Loop, keep one wave active, fast first spawn, and timing-to-half-interval override Wardenglade Three named faction spawner references per faction sequence 1 10 s Loop, keep one wave active, fast first spawn, and timing-to-half-interval override

These are authored configuration values, not measured respawn periods or a guarantee that either sequence ran in a particular match. The visible catalog data does not establish complete spawner membership, a scorer class, queue selection, or the effect of each timing flag.

Observed. TDM Courtyard / InProgress samples had no live sequence objects in one sample, a queuer instance under the mode object, and faction-paired empty waves; a later sample had active faction sequences. Adding bots filled the queuer's bot-waiting array and produced pawns while sampled wave membership stayed zero. Inferred: the mode owns that queuer as a policy; its creation was not observed.

Observed. In TDM Wardenglade / InProgress, a controlled player-death test left the player without a pawn while a faction wave gained one joined controller; a new pawn was then possessed. A control callable fired during the test, while the sampled spawn-related callables did not. This is a bounded negative result for those entry points in that sample; the function that wrote the membership is Unknown.

LTS details

Configured. Round and life settings are exposed on the mode, and level scripts reference initial spawner names and match-state presentation. The sampled catalog surface did not expose a sequence activation or queue relation, so the selected settings and path remain unestablished.

Observed. LTS Courtyard / WaitingToStart already had two inactive faction sequence objects and a queuer, with no waves. Sequences can therefore exist before activation; what activates them is Unknown.

Team Objective details

Configured. Bridgetown and Coxwell level scripts expose faction- and stage-specific spawner references, run-in-named objects, sequence calls, and both normal and forward spawn call shapes.

Unknown. The available data does not tie the sampled stage event to a concrete spawner. A receiver-specific stage path found in a different content version cannot establish this map's path or an ordinary-match forward spawn.

How to read the mode samples

Keep samples and rules separate

Each Observed statement above comes from a specific map and match state. Do not read it as a universal mode rule, and do not use it to fill the Unknown entries in the table.

For the queue policies behind these samples, see Queues and timing.

docs.title: How spawning works
docs.text: This page connects the spawning layers and marks where each handoff is established. It describes ownership and lifecycle, not a complete call trace.

docs.title: The ownership chain
docs.text:
flowchart TD S[Spawn sequenceauthority over wave order] -->|Recovered: selects| SP[Spawnercreates a wave] SP -->|Recovered: configures| W[Spawn wavemembership, timing, state] Q[Spawn queueradmission and timing policy] -.->|Inferred: policy relation| C[Controller] C -->|Recovered: can join| W W -->|Recovered: conditional end| R[Spawner releasedcleanup scheduled]

Plaintext: a sequence selects a spawner, which creates a wave. A queuer can supply controllers to that wave under its own timing policy. A controller can join the wave, and the wave's recovered end path releases the spawner when its conditions apply. This composite ownership chain is Inferred; the edge labels show which individual operations are Recovered and which relation is Inferred.

Observed sequence, not a traced edge

In the TDM Wardenglade / InProgress sample, a pawnless player was followed by a faction wave with one joined controller, then by possession of a new pawn. The native writer of that membership and the pawn-creation path were not attributed in that sample, so the diagram does not draw them as a causal handoff.

docs.title: 1. The sequence selects a spawner
docs.text:
Recovered. A sequence checks that the game mode permits spawning, that it is active, that it has spawners available, and that it is not already at its simultaneous-wave limit. It then chooses an eligible, unlocked spawner, prefers spawners that have been pushed into the candidate set, applies its timing and player-count overrides, starts the spawner, records the resulting wave, and can continue while more waves are permitted.

Unknown. Every selection tie-breaker, the activation/deactivation path in each mode, and whether a given live spawn used a sequence at all.

docs.title: 2. The spawner creates a wave
docs.text:
Recovered. A spawner refuses to start after the match or map is leaving and rejects an incompatible special spawn. Otherwise it spawns a wave, associates itself with that wave, resolves faction precedence, and applies merged parameter overrides. The wave is the spawner's active spawn job, not just a list of positions.

Unknown. Reservation, location scoring, and the exact meaning of the virtual callback a wave invokes on its spawner when it finishes.

docs.title: 3. The wave collects controllers and ends
docs.text:
Recovered. A wave exposes a joinable surface, tracks joined and previously joined controllers, replicates its state and a joined-player-state list, and holds timing and capacity settings. Its recovered join body adds a controller to the joined set, records it in controller history, removes it from the rejected set, appends that controller's player state to the replicated list, and assigns the wave as that controller's next spawn wave. Duplicate joins do not insert twice.

Recovered. The recovered end body moves an authority wave to the ending state when control is not restricted, clears the spawner's pending lock and pending-wave pointer, invokes a spawner callback, broadcasts that the wave finished, and schedules cleanup.

Unknown. The full state transition table, replication timing, refusal and leave paths, and what clients do with the replicated membership.

Wave lifecycle and live-admission boundary stateDiagram-v2 NotStarted --> Spawning: Recovered StartSpawning sets state on authority Spawning --> Ending: Recovered End on authority when control is unrestricted

Plaintext: recovered StartSpawning code sets an authority wave to spawning, but what calls that method in a particular live path remains Unknown. Recovered End code can move an authority wave to ending when control is not restricted. Other transitions, their triggers, and client-side timing remain Unknown.

A recovered callable is not the live admission path

Recovered code shows that JoinSpawn writes wave membership, and that one queuer implementation can invoke it through native virtual dispatch. In the TDM Wardenglade / InProgress respawn sample, the reflected spawn callables did not dispatch while a control callable did fire. That does not attribute the observed membership write to the recovered virtual path; the live writer remains Unknown.

docs.title: 4. The queuer is a separate policy layer
docs.text:
Recovered. Queuer variants decide admission and respawn timing: one records a per-controller accumulated delay, another uses a shared group window and diverts late entrants into a solo queue, and another records wave-timing metadata when admitting a controller. These are policies, not spawners; they do not create the wave themselves.

Recovered. One queuer implementation filters live waves for eligible player handling, world, faction, and joinability; it compares the candidates with their GetTimeLeft result, keeps the lowest result, and invokes that wave's JoinSpawn through native virtual dispatch. JoinSpawn records controller membership and the replicated player-state list. This is an implementation path, not a recorded live call.

Observed. In TDM Courtyard / InProgress and TDM Wardenglade / InProgress samples, a queuer instance was present under the mode object, including during player respawn, while its bot-waiting array stayed empty. In a TDM Courtyard / InProgress sample, a controlled bot addition filled that array and produced pawns while sampled wave membership stayed zero. An LTS Courtyard / WaitingToStart sample also had a queuer but no waves.

Inferred. Its placement under the mode object suggests it is that mode's admission/timing policy. Mode creation was not observed.

Unknown. Whether the sampled respawn used the recovered queuer-to-join path, which queuer variant a given mode actually uses for players, the meaning or units of the GetTimeLeft result, and how solo entries are promoted or cancelled.

docs.title: 5. The observable player handoff
docs.text:
Observed. In the TDM Wardenglade / InProgress sample, a controlled player-death test left the player without a pawn while a faction wave gained one joined controller. A new pawn was then possessed. The wave belonged to an authored run-in spawner, and the queuer's bot-waiting array was empty throughout.

This diagram records successive observed states, not a confirmed controller-to-wave-to-pawn call chain:

flowchart LR P["Player without pawn"] -->|"later snapshot"| W["Faction wave: one joined controller"] W -->|"later snapshot"| N["New pawn possessed"]

Plaintext: in the TDM Wardenglade / InProgress controlled death sample, the player was first pawnless, a faction wave then held one joined controller, and the player later possessed a new pawn. The native function that wrote wave membership and the path that created the pawn remain Unknown; the arrows represent time order only.

Worked example: observed respawn and recovered path Evidence What it establishes What it does not establish Observed — TDM Wardenglade / InProgress A player was without a pawn; a faction wave then had one joined controller; a new pawn was later possessed. Which function wrote membership, created the pawn, or selected that wave. Recovered — NewSpawnSystemQueuer request path The queuer can filter eligible waves, compare their GetTimeLeft results, choose the lowest-result wave, and request JoinSpawn through native virtual dispatch. That this request path ran in the Wardenglade sample, or that its timing result predicts pawn arrival. Recovered — JoinSpawn That method records controller membership/history and a replicated joined-player-state entry. That it was the observed writer, or that its bookkeeping by itself creates a pawn.

Plaintext: the live sample supplies an order of visible changes. The recovered code supplies a possible admission path and its bookkeeping. They describe compatible facts, but available evidence does not connect them into one traced call chain.

Unknown. The native function that wrote the membership, where the pawn was created, and when player control was released.

Reading boundaries Established Not established Sequence eligibility checks and spawner selection Activation and selection in every mode Spawner wave creation and configuration Location scoring and reservations Wave join/end bookkeeping Full state machine and replication timing Distinct queue admission policies Due-entry dispatch and mode ownership One observed death-to-pawn handoff The native path that produced it

For the per-component inventory, see Components; for what the evidence does not support, see Evidence and limitations.

docs.title: Queues and timing
docs.text: Queuers are admission and timing policies. They decide which controller is recorded for a future spawn and how long that controller waits; they do not create the wave themselves.

docs.title: Three recovered policies
docs.text:
Policy Admission rule Timing model Recovered cancellation behavior Wave spawn queuer Requires an active, eligible queue; rejects a controller already recorded. Records respawn/wave timing metadata for the controller and adjusts the following wave schedule. A recovered removal method searches the recorded entries and erases matching controllers. Cumulative queuer Requires an active queue and eligibility; rejects duplicates. Starts from a beginning respawn time; a controller with history instead uses the recorded value plus an accumulated increment. Unknown for its removal path. Group queuer Requires an active, valid, eligible controller; treats membership in either of its two arrays as already admitted. Uses a shared group window. Entrants while the window is still open join the active group; later entrants go to a separate solo queue. The recovered removal method searches only active group participants, not the solo queue.

Recovered. The cumulative policy is per-controller and grows with each recorded respawn. The group policy is shared across participants and explicitly separates late entrants. These are different policies, not two names for the same timer.

Unknown. What consumes a due entry, how a solo entry is promoted into a group or spawned on its own, whether another cancellation route covers solo entries, and which mode uses which deferred-queue policy for players.

Admission is not a spawn

Being recorded in a queue means the policy accepted the controller. It is not proof of a wave join or of a pawn being created. The step from a due entry to an actual spawn is not established.

Cumulative timing expression \[ d_{\mathrm{next}} = \begin{cases} d_{\mathrm{start}}, & \text{when the controller has no recorded cumulative delay} \\ d_{\mathrm{previous}} + d_{\mathrm{increment}}, & \text{when it has recorded history} \end{cases} \qquad t_{\mathrm{due}} = t_{\mathrm{now}} + d_{\mathrm{next}} \]

Plaintext: when the cumulative queuer accepts a controller, it records the configured starting delay for that controller's first recorded admission. On a later admission, it records the controller's previous delay plus the configured cumulative increment. It also records a due world time by adding that chosen delay to the current world time. This is a recovered admission rule, not a measured pawn-arrival time or a schedule for every wave and mode.

Additional timing and queue evidence

A separate recovered queuer path

NewSpawnSystemQueuer is not one of the three deferred policies above. Its recovered request path filters eligible waves, compares their GetTimeLeft results, and invokes JoinSpawn on the lowest-result wave through native virtual dispatch. This establishes an implementation path for that queuer, not that the path ran during an observed player respawn or that it consumes due entries from the three policies above.

Configured. Level and class setup exposes timing knobs such as wave interval, number of simultaneous waves, looping, keeping one wave active, a fast first spawn, a minimum wait time, and a pre-spawn delay. Different maps author different values. These settings describe the configured schedule; they do not by themselves show that a schedule was followed in a particular match.

Observed — ordinary player respawn. In the TDM Wardenglade / InProgress sample, a controlled player-death test left the player without a pawn while a faction wave gained one joined controller, and then a new pawn appeared. A queuer instance was present with an empty bot-waiting array throughout. This is one sample, not a general admission rule.

Observed — controlled bot test. In the TDM Courtyard / InProgress sample, adding a large number of bots filled the queuer's bot-waiting array immediately and produced bot pawns over the following samples, while sampled wave membership stayed at zero. Removing the bots returned the world to its earlier state. This demonstrates a bot-admission surface; it does not establish the ordinary player-respawn path.

Observed — wave objects are transient. TDM Courtyard / InProgress and TDM Wardenglade / InProgress samples showed waves appearing or rotating among placed spawners; an empty wave in one snapshot is not evidence that waves never hold players. By contrast, the LTS Courtyard / WaitingToStart sample had two inactive sequences and a queuer but no waves. A pre-round absence is not a claim about LTS during play.

Timing questions that remain open Question Status Which code consumes due entries from the wave, cumulative, or group queues? Unknown Which deferred-queue policy does each mode use for players? Unknown How are solo-queue entries promoted or cancelled? Unknown What are the real wave-state transitions on a client? Unknown When is player control released during the spawn? Unknown Do the configured intervals and delays describe the live schedule exactly? Unknown

For the configured values by mode, see Game modes. For the evidence behind each label, see Evidence and limitations.

docs.title: Evidence and limitations
docs.text: Spawning has several layers, and different evidence establishes different things. This page keeps the guide precise about what is known, what is configured, what was seen, and what remains open.

docs.title: Evidence labels
docs.text: Label Meaning Observed Seen in a documented live match or controlled test. Configured Present in an authored level, class, or default configuration. Declared A header lists a class, member, or interface; it is not recovered runtime behavior. Recovered Established implementation behavior, described here in player-facing terms. Inferred A supported working explanation that has not been fully traced. Unknown Not established by the available evidence.

docs.title: Current model at a glance
docs.text:
Topic What is established Important limit Sequence selection Eligibility, activity, concurrency, and unlocked-spawner checks are recovered. All tie-breakers and per-mode activation are not mapped. Spawner wave creation Post-match and special-spawn rejection, wave creation, faction precedence, and overrides are recovered. Location scoring and reservations are not described. Wave membership A recovered JoinSpawn body records joined and historical controllers plus a replicated joined-player-state list; a recovered end body releases the spawner. The live writer in the TDM Wardenglade / InProgress respawn was not attributed. Wave state Not started, spawning, and ending are named states; an authority wave can reach ending. The full transition table and replication timing are unknown. Queue admission Cumulative, group, and wave queues have distinct admission and timing rules. Due-entry dispatch and solo-queue handling are unknown. Queue-to-join path NewSpawnSystemQueuer filters eligible waves, compares GetTimeLeft, and invokes JoinSpawn on the lowest-result candidate through a native virtual call (Recovered). It was not recorded in the sampled respawn; the score's meaning and live attribution are Unknown. Observed queuer A queuer instance appeared under the mode in TDM Courtyard / InProgress, TDM Wardenglade / InProgress, and LTS Courtyard / WaitingToStart samples, with an empty bot-waiting array. Mode ownership is Inferred. Its role in ordinary player admission is not established. Bot admission A controlled bot addition in TDM Courtyard / InProgress filled the queuer's bot-waiting array and produced pawns. That is a bot surface, not the ordinary player-respawn path. Player respawn TDM Wardenglade / InProgress showed a pawnless player, a wave with one joined controller, then a new pawn. The native function that wrote that membership and created the pawn was not attributed in that sample. Authored spawner behavior Base and run-in spawners configure presentation, movement, and control-restriction checks. Which authored path runs in an ordinary spawn is not established. Mode differences FFA, TDM, LTS, and TO author different sequences, spawners, and timing values. One sample per mode cannot establish a universal mode rule. Team Objective forward spawns Stage scripts reference forward spawning and run-in spawners. The sampled map's stage-to-spawner receiver binding is unknown. What not to infer Why some questions remain unknown Kind of gap Example Safe interpretation No attributed live path A wave gains a member, but the writing function was not identified. Report the visible sequence and name the writer Unknown. Negative result with a control Sampled callables do not fire while a control callable does. State the negative result for those callables in that sample only. Incomplete static surface A deferred queue policy admits controllers, but its due-entry consumer is not recovered. Describe admission, not the full spawn. Incomplete map evidence A stage event cannot be bound to a concrete spawner in the sampled map data. Keep the stage reference as configured and the receiver as Unknown. Single-sample evidence One map shows a sequence or queuer in a specific match state. State the map and state; do not infer a mode-wide rule. Open questions
  1. Did the observed player respawn use the recovered NewSpawnSystemQueuer → JoinSpawn path, and which native function creates the pawn?
  2. What activates a queue and selects a spawner and wave in each mode?
  3. What are the full wave-state transitions and replication timing?
  4. How do deferred queue entries reach a wave, and how are solo-queue entries promoted or cancelled?
  5. Do FFA, TDM, LTS, and TO differ in selection and scoring, or only in authored configuration?
  6. Which authored run-in spawner paths run in ordinary player spawns, and when is control released?
  7. Which spawn data is authoritative, replicated, or only local presentation and mode state?
  8. Does LTS bypass, constrain, or use the shared sequence/spawner/wave path?
  9. Which concrete spawner does a Team Objective stage select in the sampled map?
  10. How far do these bounded samples generalize to other maps and match states?
How to use the guide responsibly
  • To know what a spawner can do, read Components and Spawner types with the Configured label in mind.
  • To understand the ownership model, read How spawning works and treat Inferred steps as a working model.
  • To check timing and queue behavior, read Queues and timing.
  • To compare modes, read Game modes and keep each Observed claim with its sample.
  • When a result matters for a new system, measure it in the context where it will be used. This guide is a map of known surfaces and their limits, not a substitute for measuring a live spawn.

docs.title: A configured spawner is not a selected spawner
docs.text: A level script can author a sequence reference, a faction sequence, a run-in spawner, or a forward spawn call. That is an inventory of what the map is equipped to do. It does not prove that a given death or objective advanced through that exact actor.

docs.title: A recovered callable is not a recorded call
docs.text: Recovered implementation bodies establish what the game is capable of doing and how an operation is structured. They do not prove that a particular callable ran in a particular match. A body that can add a controller to a wave is not, by itself, the writer of an observed membership change.

docs.title: A missing call at one entry point is not a whole-path explanation
docs.text: In the TDM Wardenglade / InProgress respawn sample, several spawn-related callables produced no events while a control callable did fire. That supports a bounded negative result for those entry points. It does not identify the function that actually performed the spawn, and it should not be generalized to every respawn.

docs.title: An empty wave is not a never-used wave
docs.text: Wave objects appear and rotate across placed spawners. A snapshot with zero joined controllers says only that the wave was empty at that moment. It is not evidence that membership cannot change later.

docs.title: A controlled test is not every match
docs.text: Bot-addition and player-death tests isolate one condition in one world at one time. Ordinary matches add objectives, teammates, attacks, timing, and other game state. Read a controlled result as evidence for the tested relationship, not as a complete model of spawning.

docs.title: Chivalry 2 stages and rounds
docs.text: If you are inspecting a map or making a mod, the first question is whether the mode expects a stage actor from the level or owns its own match lifecycle. This section explains how sampled Chivalry 2 matches move toward a result. It covers the stage actors used by Free-for-All (FFA), Team Deathmatch (TDM), and Team Objective (TO), alongside the native round state observed in Last Team Standing (LTS) and Arena.

docs.title: Start here
docs.text:
Read the TL;DR first.

The smallest useful model is not one universal stage system:

  1. In the sampled FFA and TO maps, placed stage actors were active.
  2. In sampled TDM, the mode created its ticket stage at runtime.
  3. In sampled LTS and Arena, native round and life state was visible on the game mode and game state; no stage-interface actor was observed in those bounded samples.

These are observations of representative maps, not a classification rule for every Chivalry 2 map.

The guide's most important reading rule

A configured hook, placed actor, or decoded implementation is not proof that it ran in an ordinary match. This guide marks whether a claim is Configured, Recovered, Observed, or Unknown, and identifies controlled and accelerated observations rather than presenting them as normal gameplay.

Recovered Established from a validated native implementation. It describes what that implementation does, not necessarily a live caller. Observed Measured in a live match. The surrounding text says whether it was an ordinary bot-driven run, an accelerated expiry, or a controlled trigger. Unknown Not established by the available evidence.

docs.title: Scope
docs.text: The guide describes selected FFA, TDM, LTS, Arena, and TO maps. It does not claim that their authoring or terminal behavior applies to every map, nor does it document experiment procedures, raw implementation details, or player-facing strategies.

docs.title: Endings and successor handoff
docs.text: A terminal condition and a visible successor are separate questions. A stage can return an object, make itself ready, or end a match without all modes installing the same kind of current successor.

docs.title: Which paths actually installed a successor?
docs.text:
flowchart TB subgraph FFA["FFA · controlled calls and setup"] DIRECT["Direct CompleteStage"] --> RETURNED["Candidate object returned"] RETURNED -->|"same sample"| DIRECT_CURRENT["Current stage unchanged"] SCORE["Score-limit dispatch"] -->|"entered"| POST["WaitingPostMatch"] SCORE -->|"same score-limit sample"| SCORE_CURRENT["Timeout stage still current"] end subgraph HANDOFF["TDM / TO · controlled triggers"] TRIGGER["Draw trigger or score threshold"] --> READY["Normal readiness loop"] READY --> INSTALLED["Successor installed as current"] end

Plaintext: a direct FFA completion returned a candidate without installing it; in a separate controlled FFA score-limit match, post-match began with the timeout stage still current. In sampled TDM draw and TO score tests, controlled triggers reached the normal readiness loop and a successor became current. These are distinct experiments, not one universal path or evidence that the same gameplay event invokes them in an ordinary match.

The table also includes accelerated timer expiry and a bot-driven Arena round, which are different kinds of observation:

Mode Trigger examined What was observed Boundary FFA Accelerated component expiry The timeout path completed the sampled match and reached post-match. This establishes component expiry under accelerated game time, not real-time pacing. FFA Direct completion with written kill totals Tie and unique-leader branches returned candidate sudden-death or victory objects. A returned object did not become current in this direct-call test. FFA Controlled score-limit setup The award path fired and the match reached post-match while the timeout stage remained current. Do not generalize this captured path to every FFA map or ordinary player kill. TDM Direct draw trigger The draw flag made the stage ready; after a linger, a draw stage became current and post-match began. The natural caller of draw is unknown. TDM Controlled ticket exhaustion Terminal flags made the stage ready and ended the sampled match. Ticket values were written for the test. TO Controlled score thresholds The normal readiness loop installed each successor through the fifth stage, then attacker victory. Score sources were written directly; ordinary objectives are unknown. TO Accelerated stage-1 expiry A defender victory stage became current. Later-stage timeout behavior is unknown. Arena Ordinary bot-driven 3v3 deaths Life changes, a round-win broadcast, post-match, and podium were observed. The native victory caller was not directly observed. Arena Direct round-victory call The call ended a one-round test, or reached intermission and round 2 after the round count was changed for the test. This is controlled callable behavior, not ordinary kill dispatch.

docs.title: The FFA exception
docs.text:
The sampled TDM draw and TO score paths installed a new current stage through their readiness loop. FFA did not provide a universal counterpart:

  • Direct FFA completion returned a candidate object without changing the current stage.
  • The captured controlled FFA score-limit path entered post-match while the timeout stage remained current.

The recovered native base of the FFA award method is a virtual forwarder. Its override and the selected victor's behavior remain Unknown. The safe conclusion is not “FFA installs no successor,” but “the sampled FFA paths did not show a current victory-stage installation.”

docs.title: Reading controlled results
docs.text:
Controlled observations are useful because they show how a known terminal surface responds. They do not establish what ordinary play invokes:

  • Direct score, ticket, or round-victory changes do not identify the normal gameplay event that produces them.
  • Accelerated expiry shows that an active timer can reach its terminal state; it does not measure normal pacing.
  • A bot-driven round establishes its observed team-state sequence, not a human-player combat or respawn rule.

See Evidence, limits, and terminology for the remaining Unknowns.

docs.title: Evidence, limits, and terminology
docs.text: This section documents sampled maps and bounded observations. It is designed to be useful without turning available configuration or a controlled probe into a universal game rule.

docs.title: How to read the labels
docs.text:
Label Meaning Configured Authored world settings, serialized actors, level hooks, or defaults. This shows an available setup, not necessarily live dispatch. Recovered A validated native implementation. This says what the recovered body does, not which ordinary event called it. Observed A live measurement. It is qualified as bot-driven ordinary state, controlled trigger, or accelerated expiry where that matters. Unknown The available evidence does not establish it.

Here ordinary means that the measured outcome was not directly written for the test. An ordinary bot-driven round is still not evidence about human combat or about every map.

docs.title: Important limits
docs.text:
• Representative maps only: one sampled map per mode does not establish cross-map authoring or lifecycle generality.
  • Controlled versus ordinary: direct score, ticket, method, or round-count changes reveal a response path; they do not identify an ordinary gameplay caller.
  • Single-process observations: authority order, replication delay, and RepNotify timing need a multi-client or server/client comparison.
  • Bounded negative results: no stage-interface actor was observed in the sampled LTS/Arena reads; that does not prove absence across those modes.

docs.title: What remains unknown
docs.text:
Area Unknown FFA Ordinary score-limit kill dispatch, selected victor, natural tied-score sudden death, and the virtual award override's effect. TDM The natural caller of draw, exact killer/victim pairing and faction-loss rule for ticket changes, and ordinary defeat/draw selection. Arena and LTS The exact native life writer and ordinary victory caller, all faction-selection branches, LTS scored-stage instantiation, and level round-event dispatch. TO Ordinary objective score sources, draw usage, and timeout behavior for stages 2–5. Networking Authority ordering and replication/RepNotify timing. Maps Whether the sampled behavior generalizes to other maps in each mode.

The observed Arena bot round did establish per-faction life-pool decrements and a round-win/post-match sequence. Its native writer and caller remain unknown; do not replace the observed result with a broader negative claim.

Glossary Term Meaning in this guide Stage A mode-owned lifecycle unit that can start, become ready, and provide a possible next state. Round The native Arena-derived lifecycle observed in sampled LTS and Arena modes. Ticket A per-faction count used by the sampled TDM ticket stage. Timeout stage A stage whose relevant readiness path is duration expiry. Victory stage A terminal or result-stage object that may become current in some sampled handoffs. Transition stage A stage used as transition or warmup context before another active stage. Current stage The stage presently exposed by a staged mode. A returned object is not automatically current. Readiness The condition that permits a stage to complete; its source differs by implementation.

docs.title: Stage and round authoring surfaces
docs.text: Modder's question: when inspecting a map, which values belong in World Settings, which actors or level hooks supply a stage, and which state belongs to the game mode? These are configured examples from sampled shipped maps, not a tested checklist for making a new map. In particular, the presence of a hook does not show that an ordinary match calls it.

docs.title: Start with the map's World Settings
docs.text:
TBL World Settings exposes DefaultGameMode and an instanced GameModeSettings object derived from TBLGameModeSettings. Choose a settings object that matches the chosen mode; do not infer the mode from a map-name prefix alone. World Settings also exposes stage-ending configuration and warmup/sequence surfaces, but their exact use depends on the mode and map.

Sampled map Configured game mode Settings or round values to inspect First-stage responsibility FFA Tournament Grounds Mode_FFA_C Settings_FFA_C: score limit and match duration; defaults include score 35 and 900 seconds, with player-count scaling available. Level GetFirstStage returns the placed FFATimeoutStage_C. TDM Tournament Grounds Mode_TDM_C Settings_TDM_C: tickets and match duration; the sample started with 75 per faction and 600 seconds. The mode creates TDMStage_C from its settings; the level exposes Start TDM Stage, not a placed ticket stage. TO Bridgetown StagedGameMode_C UseNewStageIdNumbers, stage-ending configuration, and scored-stage initialization values; no GameModeSettings reference was present in this export. Level GetFirstStage initializes and returns the first of five placed scored stages. LTS Tournament Grounds Native LTSGameMode LTSGameModeSettings on World Settings; round count, lives, and delays are fields on the Arena-derived mode. Native round state was observed; a level stage-start hook exists but its ordinary dispatch is unknown. Arena Courtyard Native ArenaGameMode ArenaGameModeSettings on World Settings; round count, lives, and timing belong to the native mode. Round events and a stage-start hook are authored; no stage-interface actor was observed in the bounded match.

Configured values are not guaranteed gameplay results. For example, FFA and TDM settings can scale values by player count; a default in an asset is not necessarily the active value in a different match.

docs.title: How the sampled staged maps provide a first stage
docs.text:
GetFirstStage is the level Blueprint interface entry used by the sampled FFA and TO staged maps. For FFA, the level returns a placed timeout-stage actor of the expected class. A decoded FFA branch can create a fallback timeout stage if the level result is absent or unsuitable; no sampled map was observed using the fallback. Do not treat that fallback as permission to omit the level setup from an untested new map.

For TDM, the sampled level did not place a TDMStage_C. The mode created and initialized one from Settings_TDM_C and exposed a Start TDM Stage level hook. Its presence in the map is Configured; this guide does not assert when that hook ran in an ordinary match.

For TO Bridgetown, GetFirstStage initializes five placed ScoredStage_C actors, wires score-successor and timeout destinations, and returns stage 1. The following table describes its authored initialization, not ordinary objective progress or a recommendation for other maps:

Placed stage Stage ID Initial/max score Duration On score / on timeout 1 10 0 / 1000 330 s Stage 2 / defender victory 2 20 0 / 1000 300 s Stage 3 / defender victory 3 30 0 / 3500 240 s Stage 4 / defender victory 4 40 0 / 1200 300 s Stage 5 / defender victory 5 50 0 / 1300 300 s Attacker victory / defender victory

These score and duration values come from the level's initialization graph, not simply the placed actors' serialized defaults. A controlled test advanced the score branch through all five stages, while an accelerated stage-1 timeout installed defender victory. Ordinary objective-to-score sources, later timeout outcomes, and behavior on another TO map are unknown.

Transition stage and stage-ending configuration

A staged-mode path can wrap the level's first stage in a transition stage using World Settings warmup and spawner-binding surfaces. The sampled TO match had a transition stage as its previous stage, but that observation does not identify which construction path produced the instance.

Bridgetown configures UseNewStageIdNumbers and a last-stage ID of 50. The stage-ending configuration and the placed stages' IDs are separate surfaces. Do not copy these numbers into another map without checking its authored chain and mode configuration.

docs.title: Native rounds are not staged-map recipes
docs.text:
ArenaGameMode declares Rounds, TeamLives, FinalLives, TimeBetweenRounds, RoundTimeLimit, and PreCountdownDelay; LTSGameMode derives from it. LTSGameModeSettings also exposes optional round-count override fields. The sampled Arena map has three initial spawners per faction and a configured round time limit of zero; its bot-driven round was untimed. Neither a generic maximum-player value nor adding a bot to start a probe establishes the authoring requirements of a 1v1 map.

No LTSScoredStage_C was found in the sampled LTS match, and the authored level Start TDM Stage or round-event bindings do not prove ordinary dispatch. Inspect the actual mode, settings, and level event wiring before adapting a native-round map.

Not a verified new-map recipe

These examples identify shipped-map configuration and a few bounded live results. They do not establish every required field, hook consumer, spawn arrangement, replication rule, or success condition for a new map. Validate your own map and match state rather than assuming a copied setup will run.

For runtime ownership see Stage and round overview; for timing and completion see Timers and readiness and Endings and handoff.

docs.title: Sampled native-round modes: LTS and Arena
docs.text: The sampled LTS and Arena matches exposed native round configuration on Arena-derived game modes and live team-life state in the game state. This is different from the active stage actors observed in the sampled FFA, TDM, and TO matches. For the settings classes and fields to inspect when authoring a map, see Map authoring surfaces.

docs.title: Map supplies
docs.text: Configured: the sampled map selected native LTS settings. Its level also contained authored stage-start-related surfaces, but their dispatch was not established.

docs.title: Mode owns
docs.text: Observed: the match used native round fields such as round number, lives, and round delays. No stage-interface actor was found in the bounded sample.

docs.title: Observed
docs.text:
The sampled match advanced through preparation and first-round countdown into play after an additional participant joined. That does not establish a required team size for a custom LTS map.

Why the startup sample is limited

The initial one-player setup did not progress until a bot was added. The intervention is a test condition, not an authored minimum-player rule or evidence about which round events are dispatched.

docs.title: Unknown
docs.text: The ordinary round-end owner and life writer, LTS scored-stage instantiation, and level round-event dispatch remain unknown.

docs.title: Map supplies
docs.text: Configured: the sampled Arena map selected native Arena settings and had three initial spawners per faction. It is therefore 3v3-shaped; a generic maximum-player setting is not a 1v1 rule.

docs.title: Mode owns
docs.text: Observed: native round number, per-faction lives, and round-victory state were active. Configured: the map's round time limit was zero; this bot-driven round had no round countdown to observe.

docs.title: Observed
docs.text: In an ordinary bot-driven 3v3 round, the per-faction life pool fell with deaths, a round-win broadcast occurred, and the match moved through post-match to the victory podium. The local player had no spawned pawn, so this supports team-life and victory-state observations, not human combat or respawn claims.

docs.title: Observed Arena round sequence
docs.text:
This is a sequence of observed bot-match states, not a recovered native call chain:

flowchart TB PREP["PreparingMatch"] --> COUNT["FirstRoundStartCountdown"] COUNT --> PLAY["InProgress · faction lives (2, 2)"] PLAY -->|"bot deaths; lives fell to (1, 0)"| WON["Round-win broadcast"] WON --> POST["WaitingPostMatch"] POST --> PODIUM["VictoryPodium"]

Plaintext: in the sampled Arena 3v3 bot match, preparation led to a first-round countdown and play; the faction life pools fell from (2, 2) to (1, 0), then a round-win broadcast was recorded before post-match and the victory podium. The broadcaster's ordinary native caller and the exact life writer were not identified. The separate direct victory-call experiment below is not an arrow in this observed sequence.

Controlled comparison: direct round-victory call

A separate direct round-victory call ended a single-round configuration. When the round count was changed for the test, the direct call instead entered intermission and began round 2. This is evidence about the controlled callable path, not an observed five-round map configuration or ordinary kill dispatch.

docs.title: Unknown
docs.text:
The exact native writer and ordinary caller of the victory path, faction selection in all branches, and level round-event dispatch remain unknown. The ordinary bot run did not directly confirm the round-victory method hook.

See Endings and handoff for why direct calls and ordinary state transitions remain separate evidence.

docs.title: Stage and round overview
docs.text: A stage is a mode-owned unit that can start, decide whether it is ready to finish, and produce a possible next state. A round is the native Arena-derived lifecycle used in the sampled LTS and Arena matches. The names describe different ownership models in the evidence available here; they are not interchangeable labels for every map.

docs.title: The sampled ownership split
docs.text:
Sampled mode family What owned the active lifecycle What was observed FFA A placed timeout stage under a staged game mode The placed stage was active during the sampled match. TDM A ticket stage created by the mode A dynamic ticket stage was active; no placed ticket-stage actor was needed in the sampled map. TO Placed scored stages under a staged game mode The first placed scored stage became current after a transition stage. LTS and Arena Native Arena-derived round/life state Native round fields were active; no stage-interface actor was found in the bounded samples.

This is an Observed comparison of one representative map per mode. It does not prove that another map cannot use a different setup.

docs.title: What a staged mode can expose
docs.text:
Declared: the stage interface includes operations for starting a stage, checking readiness, reporting time and identity, and completing a stage. Configured: levels can provide a first-stage hook, while World Settings can select a default game mode and a mode settings object.

Those surfaces describe what the game is equipped to use. They do not show that a particular hook or branch ran in the sampled match. For example, a level can contain a stage-start hook without evidence that the native-round LTS or Arena sample dispatched it.

docs.title: Current, previous, and next
docs.text:
In the sampled staged modes, the game mode can expose a current stage and, after a handoff, a previous stage. A stage can report completion and supply a candidate next state. What the mode does with that result is mode-specific: some sampled TDM and TO readiness paths installed a successor as current, while the captured FFA score-limit path entered post-match with its timeout stage still current.

Warning

Do not turn “a stage returned an object” into “the object became current.” The direct FFA completion experiment returned a victory object without changing the current stage. See Endings and handoff.

docs.title: Transition and warmup context
docs.text:
Configured / decoded: the staged-mode setup includes a transition-stage path that can wrap or precede a first stage, using level and world-settings configuration. Observed: the sampled TO match had a transition stage as its previous stage when its first scored stage was current.

The observation does not independently establish which construction path made that transition instance. It is therefore safer to say that a transition stage was present in the sample than to claim every TO map uses the same warmup path.

docs.title: Native round context
docs.text:
Observed: sampled LTS and Arena matches exposed round number, rounds, and life-related state on native Arena-derived modes and their game state. This guide calls that a native-round lifecycle to separate it from the active stage actors observed in FFA, TDM, and TO.

No stage-interface actor was observed in the bounded LTS/Arena reads. That is a limited observation, not proof that such an actor never exists in those modes. See Native-round modes for the relevant boundaries.

For the fields and hooks a modder can inspect in the sampled maps, see Map authoring surfaces.

docs.title: Sampled staged modes: FFA, TDM, and TO
docs.text: These panels separate what the sampled map supplied from what the mode created or used at runtime. They do not turn one map into a rule for every map. For specific World Settings, hooks, and TO initialization values, see Map authoring surfaces.

docs.title: Map supplies
docs.text: Configured: the sampled FFA map selected its FFA game mode and settings, and its level provided a placed timeout stage through the first-stage surface.

docs.title: Mode creates or uses
docs.text: Observed: that placed timeout stage was active in the sampled match. Decoded: the mode also has a fallback path that can create a timeout stage when a suitable level result is unavailable. No sampled map was observed using that fallback.

docs.title: Observed
docs.text:
• The placed stage ran with a component countdown of about fifteen minutes.
  • Accelerated component expiry completed the sampled match.
  • A controlled score-limit setup dispatched the FFA award path and reached post-match while the timeout stage remained current.

docs.title: Unknown
docs.text: An ordinary player-driven score-limit kill, the selected victor, the virtual award override, and natural tied-score sudden-death dispatch remain unknown. The score-limit path is separate from timeout-stage readiness; see Timers and readiness.

docs.title: Map supplies
docs.text: Configured: the sampled map selected TDM settings and a level stage-start surface. It did not contain a placed ticket-stage actor.

docs.title: Mode creates or uses
docs.text: Observed: the mode created and used a dynamic ticket stage with a 600-second component timer and 75 tickets per tracked faction in the sample.

docs.title: Observed
docs.text:
• Component expiry completed the sampled match under accelerated game time.
  • A bot-match kill handler coincided with single-ticket decrements, without direct ticket edits.
  • Controlled ticket exhaustion and a controlled draw trigger made terminal readiness paths available.

docs.title: Unknown
docs.text: The exact death pairing and faction-loss rule for the observed ticket changes are not established; the capture included additional attempted death triggers whose contribution could not be isolated. The natural caller of the draw path and ordinary defeat/draw selection also remain unknown.

docs.title: Map supplies
docs.text: Configured: the sampled TO map contained five placed scored stages and configured successor and timeout outcomes. A transition stage was also present as the previous stage when the first scored stage was current.

docs.title: Mode creates or uses
docs.text: Observed: the staged mode made the placed scored stages current in sequence. The presence of a transition instance does not prove which configured warmup path created it.

docs.title: Observed
docs.text: With each current stage set to its configured score threshold, the normal readiness path advanced through stages 1–5 and reached an attacker victory stage. An accelerated timeout of stage 1 installed a defender victory stage.

docs.title: Bridgetown stage flow
docs.text:
The arrows below show two different kinds of evidence on this one map. The solid score route was Observed with controlled score writes; the stage-1 timeout route was Observed with accelerated expiry. The level configures timeout destinations for stages 2–5, but those outcomes were not observed and are not drawn as tested transitions.

flowchart TB S1["Stage 1 · ID 10"] -->|"score threshold · controlled"| S2["Stage 2 · ID 20"] S2 -->|"score threshold · controlled"| S3["Stage 3 · ID 30"] S3 -->|"score threshold · controlled"| S4["Stage 4 · ID 40"] S4 -->|"score threshold · controlled"| S5["Stage 5 · ID 50"] S5 -->|"score threshold · controlled"| ATK["Attacker victory · current"] S1 -->|"timeout · accelerated"| DEF["Defender victory · current"]

Plaintext: in a controlled Bridgetown run, setting each current stage's score to its configured maximum moved the current stage from 1 to 2, 3, 4, 5 and then attacker victory. Separately, accelerating stage 1's timer expiry installed defender victory. The arrows do not identify ordinary objective score sources or establish later-stage timeout behavior. The authoring table lists all configured score and timeout destinations.

docs.title: Unknown
docs.text:
The ordinary objective events that supply score, draw usage, timeout behavior for stages 2–5, and cross-map behavior remain unknown. The controlled score chain establishes successor handoff, not ordinary objective progression.

For terminal-path detail, including why FFA is different from the sampled TDM and TO handoffs, see Endings and handoff.

docs.title: Timers and readiness
docs.text: The active stage or round owns the useful completion information. There is no single timer query that safely describes every sampled mode.

docs.title: Why a zero time query can mislead
docs.text:
Observed: in sampled FFA and TDM matches, a stage-level query and a native game-state time query could read zero while the active TimeObjectiveComponent still counted down. A zero result therefore does not mean the active match timer is exhausted, paused, or ready to complete.

The reader-facing rule is simple: use the timer and terminal state that belong to the active implementation, not a generic query alone.

docs.title: Readiness differs by stage type
docs.text:
Active implementation Configured / decoded readiness surface Observed boundary FFA timeout stage Duration expiry The mode's score-limit check is separate from this stage's readiness. TDM ticket stage Attacker terminal flag, defender terminal flag, or draw flag On timeout, the component's expiry event sets a terminal condition before readiness; a controlled ticket-zero or draw trigger can set one while the timer still has time left. TO scored stage Duration expiry or configured maximum score The score-successor chain was reached after controlled score changes; ordinary objective sources remain unknown. Native Arena/LTS round Native round/life fields A single generic stage timer was not established as the owner.

“Configured / decoded” identifies available logic, not an ordinary live caller. The table deliberately avoids treating the same condition as proven runtime behavior in every map.

docs.title: What was measured
docs.text:
Observed, accelerated expiry: the active FFA and TDM timer components reached zero and the matches completed. The captures establish that component expiry can drive those sampled terminal paths; they do not measure ordinary real-time pacing.

Observed, controlled terminal state: TDM ticket exhaustion and draw probes made the stage ready through terminal flags while the component still had time left. Those actions establish how the readiness path responds, not the natural event that invokes it.

Observed, controlled score: the sampled TO stage chain advanced when each current stage reached its configured score threshold. This establishes the successor behavior of that readiness route, not which ordinary objective event awards score.

docs.title: Practical interpretation
docs.text:
When reading a match state:

  1. Identify the active stage or native round owner.
  2. Read that implementation's component timer, score, lives, tickets, or terminal flags together.
  3. Treat a generic zero time result as incomplete information.
  4. Keep the cause of a terminal state separate from the fact that it became ready.

For the mode-specific ownership and limits, see Staged modes and Native-round modes. For terminal outcomes after readiness, see Endings and handoff.

docs.title: Stages and rounds TL;DR
docs.text:
Chivalry 2 does not use one identical lifecycle for every mode.

flowchart LR MAP[Sampled map setup] --> PLACED[FFA / TO: placed first stage] MAP --> DYNAMIC[TDM: mode creates ticket stage] MAP --> ROUND[LTS / Arena: native round state]

Plaintext: sampled FFA and TO maps supplied placed first stages, the sampled TDM mode created a ticket stage, and the sampled LTS and Arena matches used native round state. The diagram describes observed ownership in those maps, not a recipe or a universal rule for all maps.

  • FFA and TO: sampled maps used placed stage actors. TO's sampled map had a chain of scored stages; FFA used a placed timeout stage.
  • TDM: the sampled mode created a ticket stage from its settings instead of using a placed ticket-stage actor.
  • LTS and Arena: sampled matches exposed native round, life, and victory state rather than a stage-interface actor.

What ends a match also depends on the implementation. A stage's timer, score threshold, or terminal flag can be relevant, but a generic stage-time query may read zero while the active component timer still counts down. Read the mode and stage-specific rules rather than assuming a universal clock.

Note

Several terminal paths were measured with controlled score, ticket, or method triggers; timer expiry was sometimes accelerated. They show what a sampled path can do, not a guarantee about ordinary player-driven matches.

The most important exception is FFA: in the sampled controlled score-limit capture, the match entered post-match while its timeout stage remained current. Do not assume that every completed stage installs a visible successor as the current stage.

For the detailed boundaries and remaining questions, start with Stage and round overview, inspect map authoring surfaces if you are building a map, and finish with Evidence, limits, and terminology.

Riposte Attack immediately after a block to perform a riposte, which is a faster attack that also blocks all incoming strikes for a time. AltAttackSurprise Use {AltAttack} to alternate your attack pattern and surprise your opponent! JumpToDodge Use {Jump} while walking backwards or sideways to perform a small dodge. TeamDamage Use stabs and overheads near teammates to avoid hitting them! ChainAttacks Chain attacks together by attacking again before your current attack completes. AttacksCancelled Attacks can be canceled in windup phase, before they begin dealing damage. Press {CancelAttack}. WeaponDamageRelease Your weapon deals damage while it is in Release phase. VulnerableRecovery You are vulnerable during the recovery phase of attacks and cannot attack or parry. FeintingMissingStam Feinting, parrying, jumping and missing attacks all cost stamina. HeavyAttacks Heavy attacks deal more damage and allow you to mix up the timing and range of your strike, especially when feinting from a normal attack. DuckEnemyAttack You can duck an enemy attack by crouching and looking down or up. Press {Crouch}. FeintAttackWindup You can feint an attack in windup with {CancelAttack} to trick your enemy or to parry instead. ChangeAttackDirection Press {AltAttack} to change the initial direction of any melee swing. WASDIsFeet Think of your left hand as your feet and your right hand as your hips, turn into your strikes! Initiative2 When you land a strike or block successfully,  you have the timing advantage, so keep the pressure on by comboing! TurningTipParry Keep the tip of the enemy\'s weapon in the middle of your screen to successfully parry. GroupAttacks Attack as a group to make it easier to capture objectives! Counter Attack from block with an attack that matches your opponents strike type BEFORE it hits your block to counter. WindingUpCancel When winding up, {Parry} will cancel the attack and begin parrying. ActivateBattlecry Charge into battle screaming! Activate your Battlecry by pressing {BattleCry}! SelectClass Press {SelectClass} to change your class and weapons while in a match. ToggleCamera Press {ToggleCamera} to switch between 1st and 3rd person camera. OverlayDefaultControls Press F1 or navigate to the controls sheet in options to display an overlay of the default controls while in-game. BlockProjectiles Only shields can block arrows and bolts, but thrown weapons can be parried by any weapon. Shields can even block projectiles when on your back if you\'re clever enough. EnemyCowardThrow Is your enemy running away like a coward? All weapons can be thrown with {Throw}! DownedEnemies Killing downed enemies is an effective way to pad your score and help your team! CrawlWhileDowned Crawl to safety or fight back to your feet if downed, you can be revived and rejoin the battle! ReviveTeammates Revive downed teammates for a score reward and to bolster your numbers after a clash. ShiftToFocus Press {SHIFT} for focused aim while drawing the bow, crossbow or siege weapon. BrokenShields Shields can be damaged and broken. Hit them hard. PickUpWeapon You can pick up any weapon you see on the battlefield. ItemsUsedAsWeapon Some Items in the world can be picked up and used as a weapon. SpecialAttackBlock Special attacks will stagger a blocking opponent, leaving them unable to riposte ArrowTravel Arrows take time to travel. Lead your target by aiming where they will be, not where they are. CounterFeints You can feint a counter attempt if you make a mistake or your opponent changes their attack type Initiative When you take a hit or get blocked your opponent has the timing advantage, so block, evade or jab to recover! DamageFallOff A projectile will do less damage to targets further away. ArrowDrop Arrows will drop as they travel, aim up or down to adjust the range of your shot. DrawBow The longer you draw your bow, the more powerful the shot. HoldingDrawStam Holding an arrow drawn will cost you stamina. CounterTip A succesful counter negates the knockback and stamina loss on blocks EatingFoodDesc You can also heal by eating food items found in the map. Eat by battlecrying while holding food.

docs.title: Input Replay Component
docs.text:
Controller Component which allows you to record and replay player inputs. See UInputReplayComponent

Recorded data is written to a binary file. It can be loaded and played back on an NPC or yourself* Resulting .input files are written to %LocalAppData%\Chivalry 2\Saved\InputReplay\*.input The filename can be specified by user. This component offers other functions, for example stitching input replays together.

docs.title: What is recorded
docs.text:
• Mouse movement
  • WASD movement
  • All attacks
  • Crouch
  • Battlecry

docs.title: What isn’t recorded
docs.text: • Emotes

docs.title: Caveats
docs.text:
• By default, bots are locked to a walking state. Make sure you don’t sprint while recording
  • Turning on the spot is a bit tricky. You may need to exaggerate your turns

* by default, mouse movement overrides input replay on yourself

docs.title: Minimal Example
docs.text:
1. Add a UInputReplayComponent to your local ATBLPlayerController using the CreateInputReplayComponent node.
  2. Record a .input file using InputRec.
  3. Spawn an NPC using SpawnTBLAIFromClass and make it a dummy bot.
  4. Play the recorded file on the NPC or on yourself.

Comma-Separated list of mod actors to enable on next map --all-mod-actors --all-mod-actors GiantSlayers,… List of available mods (required for Mod Loader GUI)
  • --next-map-name ffa_wardenglade Sets the map the server will travel to after login

Comma-Separated list of mod actors (pak names) to enable on next map With this you should be able to load into the map and enable mods (you'd have to DL pak releases manually) if you want to change mods between maps, you can do servertravel to_raid?mods=FlashBlades,...

docs.title: T2 Create a Free For All Map (FFA)
1 Requirements
docs.text:
• Unreal Engine 4.25.4
  • recursively cloned version of our ArgonSDK#Repository Optional:
  • Re-generated mesh and texture assets (AssetGenerator) (so you can reuse TB’s visual assets)

docs.title: 2 Introduction
docs.text:
In this tutorial, we will create a simple FFA Map Using Sublevels (More info: UE Docs: Sublevels)

We will create 2 Sub-Levels:

  • Atmospherics (reusable)
    • Lights, Sky
  • FFA
    • Spawner

Faq

Splitting the level into these parts will allow you to reuse atmospherics in other levels, thus saving time when you’re just exploring. Alternatively you can create a single Level containing all actors in this tutorial

docs.title: 3.1 Create a new Level
docs.text:
1. Navigate to Content/Mods directory in `Content Browser
  2. Create a new folder within and open it

    (Right Click→New Folder or using the CTRL+N shortcut)

  3. Create a new Level and give it a name (e.g. Example_Atmospherics)

    Right Click → Level (Open the level after naming)

    Upon opening, your editor will look like this:

  4. Activate Atmosphere/Fog Sun Light for the Directional Light in Details window

Info

This allows you to adjust sun’s position with by moving your mouse while holding CTRL+L

docs.title: 3.2 Add lights and fog to your Scene
docs.text:
1. In the Place Actors frame, search for and drag following actors into your scene
  2. Directional Light
  3. Sky Light
  4. Exponential Height Fog
  5. Sky Atmosphere
  6. Sphere Reflection Capture

docs.title: 3.3 Reduce fog scattering (Optional)
docs.text:
• Set Directional/Fog Inscattering Color to (almost) black for the ExponentialHeightFog actor

  • Increase Fog Height Falloff to 0.6 or more

docs.title: 3.4 Use a folder to organize actors (Optional)
docs.text:
Within the World Outliner, select all actors and move them to a separate folder.

Right Click → Move To →Create New Folder

docs.title: 4.1 Create a new Level in the same directory (e.g. FFA_Example)
docs.text: Follow the steps described in 2. Don't forget to open your new level

docs.title: 4.2 Add Atmospherics Sublevel
docs.text:
1. Open the Levels window if not visible

    Window → Levels

  2. Drag-And-Drop your Atmospherics level into the list.

  3. Right-Click on the Level and change the Streaming Method to Always Loaded

  4. Double-Click the Persistent Level entry to make it the active level

docs.title: 4.3 Create a floor
docs.text:
1. Drag-and-Drop a Cube from Place Actors window into your scene

  2. Set Actor Scale values to (\(X=50, Y=50, Z=0.1\)) in the Details window

    (Optional) Apply a Material Instance of your liking (e.g. LS_StoneFloor02)

docs.title: 4.4 World Settings
docs.text:
Open World Settings window if not visible (Window→World Settings)

Adjust following Settings:

Setting Description/Value Map Name, Map Description Visible when the map loads ingame Attacking Faction FFA Gamemode Type Free for All Kill Z -5000 (this ensures that players/bots die when falling off the edge)

Make sure current Gamemode is set to Mode_FFA_C:

docs.title: 4.5 Initial Spawners
docs.text:
1. Open your Content Browser and add a BaseSpawner actor to your level

  2. Adjust it’s Row/Column count and spacing in the Details window In this example, we’ll use a 4x4 grid with a spacing of 500

    The spawner visualization will reflect changes immediately

  3. In World Settings, assign the Spawner to Attacker Initial Spawn

  4. Save your progress (CRTL+SHIFT+A to save everything)

docs.title: 4.6 Navigation Mesh (Bots)
docs.text:
A Navigation mesh will allow bots to plan their movements in the environment according to their current task.

Note

YT videos explaining UE4 NavMeshes are available in Additional Resources: Navigation

  1. Drag a Nav Mesh Bounds Volume from the Place Actors window into your scene.

  2. Scale and adjust it’s position to cover an area within your floor mesh Press P to enable mesh visualization. Orange is your friend

docs.title: 5.1 Add to the list of packaged maps
docs.text:
1. Right-Click the _Atmospherics map in Contentbrowser
    • Select Copy Reference (this will copy an internal path to clipboard)

  2. Open Project Settings

    1. Type “cook” in the search bar
    2. Add a new entry to List of maps to include in a packaged build
    3. Paste the copied reference and adjust the path. For example:
      • Copied: World'/Game/Mods/FieldGuide/Examples/Maps/Example_Atmospherics.Example_Atmospherics'
      • Target: /Game/Mods/FieldGuide/Examples/Maps/Example_Atmospherics

docs.title: 5.2 Build, Cook, Copy
docs.text:
1. Build the scene lighting by clicking on Build
  2. Save the map

    CTRL+SHIFt+S

  3. Cook the map

    File → Cook Content for Windows

    This step will create cooked assets under ArgonSDK/Saved/Cooked/WindowsNoEditor/TBL/Content/<YourFolder>

  4. (Optional) copy the cooked assets to game directory

    1. Navigate to ArgonSDK\Saved\Cooked\WindowsNoEditor\TBL\Content\
    2. Copy the Mods folder to your Game’s Content dir (Chivalry2\TBL\Content)

Note

This step is not required if your cooked Mods directory is symlinked to your game’s content directory

docs.title: 5.3 Testing your map
docs.text:
Info

The Mod Loader GUI automatically detects custom maps in the /Content/Mods directory (also those loaded from a pak file).

  1. Launch the moddable version of the game using Unchained Launcher
  2. Limit the number of bots to 15 (we only have 16 spawn slots)

  3. Select Custom in the gamemode field. Your map should now be visible in the combo box to the left

    After loading into map you should be able to spawn alongside bots.

Hint

You and the bots will spawn only once. Implementing Spawn Waves requires additional components and will be explained in next tutorial

Note

Example maps created in this tutorial are available under /Content/Mods/FieldGuide/Examples/Maps

docs.title: T3 Create your first Blueprint Mod
Requirements
docs.text:
• Unreal Engine 4.25.4
  • recursively cloned version of our ArgonSDK#Repository

docs.title: YT Example
docs.text: An example demonstrating the creation of a simple mod which executes a console command Parts related to mod loading at the end of the video are outdated!

docs.title: Working directory
docs.text:
You may create mods and maps anywhere in the Content\Mods directory.

Info

Historically, the default directory for Mod Actors is Content\Mods\AgMods\<ModName>\<ModName>.uasset. If you stick to this naming scheme, you don’t have to specify any asset when adding a Mod Marker (#2. Create a Mod Marker). Pak batch script provided in this tutorial also targets this base directory by default Content\Mods\AgMods

docs.title: 1. Create a Mod Actor
docs.text:
1. In the Content Browser window, create and enter a new directory, then right click and create a new Blueprint asset
  2. Select ArgonSDKModBase as base class when prompted.
  3. Name it as desired. Don’t use spaces

docs.title: 2. Create a Mod Marker
docs.text:
A Mod Marker is required for the mod loader to detect your newly created actor. You can use a single Mod Marker to tag multiple actors.

  1. Right-Click and create a new Data Asset (Miscellaneous -> Data Asset) of class DA_ModMarker
  2. You can leave the default filename or pick something else (e.g. ModMarker)
  3. Open the Data Asset and add your ModBase actor to Mod Actors

Info

You can omit this step if you’re using this base directory and naming scheme Content\Mods\AgMods\<ModName>\<ModName>

  • the value field is currently unused, in the future it may be displayed as part of the tooltip in main menu

docs.title: 3. Mod Settings
docs.text: Open the Mod Actor asset (MyFirstMod). A new window should open with a list of properties When inside the Blueprint editor, click on Class Defaults to view and edit these settings.

docs.title: General Settings
docs.text: Ignore Duplicate and Mod Version Repl fields. Ingame Mod Menu Widgets specifies a map of widgets to be displayed as tabs during a match. See #In-Match UI

docs.title: Mod Loader Settings
docs.text: Flag Description Silent Load Don’t show Loaded *** Version.. message during a match Online Only Only Unchained Host Only Only offline play or on an Unchained Server Allow on Frontend Load only on the Frontend map (main menu). Mod is instantly enabled when toggled Clientside Mod will load on the client only (Unchained and TB MP)

docs.title: 4. Hello World
docs.text: Let’s print something 1. Open the Mod Actor (MyFirstMod) 2. Click on Open Full Blueprint Editor if only the class defaults are visible 3. Right-Click and add a Show Local Chat node (wrapper for ClientReceiveLocalizedChat) 4. Connect it to the Parent:BeginPlay node Now as soon as the mod actor is loaded (spawned), our message will be displayed in the chat

docs.title: 5. Cooking and PAKing
docs.text: See Introduction#Loose vs Packaged assets for general description. flowchart LR subgraph Cooking and Paking a mod direction LR A("Raw Assets .uasset .umap") --> U[Unreal Engine] -- Cooking --> C("Cooked Assets .uasset .uexp .ubulk") -- UnrealPak --> E(Pak File) -- Copy--> cp[Game] end

docs.title: Option A1: Cook and Package in UE4 Editor
docs.text:
1. Locate ModPackerWidget in Content/Scripts directory and run it (Right Click -> Run) 2. Change the output directory - You can set it to the Chiv2 Paks directory. A running client will block pak replacement 3. Click on Find to locate mod markers, Cook if necessary

Note

Options A1 and A2 support content replacement. Any assets placed in _Content subdirectory inside a mod’s folder will be saved as TBL/Game/...

docs.title: Option A2: Cook and Package with Python script
docs.text:
The Widget Blueprint in #Option A1 Cook and Package in UE4 Editor is a wrapper for the build.py script located in ArgonSDK/Scripts. The script can be called manually for a more streamlined packaging process.

Supported functions are: cook, pak

docs.title: Default values
docs.text:
Open the script in a text editor and set following paths valid for your setup. This step is optional but it will let you omit some parameters when calling the script 

PROJ_PATH_DEFAULT = 'M:/chivmodding_i/SDK/ArgonSDK/TBL.uproject'

UE4_PATH_DEFAULT = 'H:/epic/UE_4.25/Engine/'

OUTPUT_DIR_DEFAULT = 'M:/chivmodding_i/SDK/ArgonSDK/Scripts'

docs.title: Cooking
docs.text:
usage: build.py cook [-h] [uproject_path] [ue4_root]

positional arguments:
  uproject_path  path to .uproject file
  ue4_root       path to ue4 ("H:/epic/UE_4.25/Engine/")

docs.title: Paking
docs.text:
usage: build.py pak [-h] mod_name [mod_dir] [dest_dir] [uproject_path] [ue4_root]

positional arguments:
  mod_name       Name of the mod (resulting pak) (or comma separated list)
  mod_dir        mod directory, base directory (ends with /) or comma-separated list. defaults to "/Game/Mods/AgMods/<mod_name>"
  dest_dir       Output directory. Will be created on spawn
  uproject_path  path to .uproject file
  ue4_root       path to ue4 ("H:/epic/UE_4.25/Engine/")

Single mod: python build.py pak DripSync will create DripSync.pak from source in /Game/Mods/AgMods Multiple mods (these commands yield same results): 

$ python build.py pak DripSync,ModMenu /Game/Mods/AgMods/DripSync,/Game/Mods/AgMods/ModMenu 
$ python build.py pak DripSync,ModMenu /Game/Mods/AgMods/ 
$ python build.py pak DripSync,ModMenu

Mod "DripSync": "/Game/Mods/AgMods/DripSync"
27 files added to "M:/chivmodding_i/SDK/ArgonSDK/Scripts\DripSync.pak"
Mod "ModMenu": "/Game/Mods/AgMods/ModMenu"
36 files added to "M:/chivmodding_i/SDK/ArgonSDK/Scripts\ModMenu.pak"

docs.title: Option B: Cook and Package with a Batch script
docs.text:
Warning

This method is suitable if:

  • Your mods are located in Content\Mods\AgMods\<ModName> directory (naming not important)
  • Your mod has no asset replacements (e.g. Heraldry replacement)
  1. Locate build.bat in ArgonSDK\Scripts\build.bat
    • ArgonSDK github: build.bat
  2. Edit your local file and set CHIVALRY_PATH and UE4_PATH variables`_ 
    set "CHIVALRY_PATH=I:\Epic Games\Chivalry2_c\TBL\Content\Paks"
 set "UE4_PATH=I:\Epic Games\UE_4.25\Engine\Binaries\Win64"

Optionally create a shortcut and set CHIV2_LAUNCH_LNK variable to launch the game with -l parameter set "CHIV2_LAUNCH_LNK=I:\Epic Games\Chivalry 2 - EGS.url" 3. Run the script using following syntax: build.bat <ModName> -c -l -c : also cook the project -l : launch game after paking

e.g. build.bat DeathRecap -c followed by build.bat ModMenu -l to cook both and launch afterwards

Info

The script will create a new output directory under ArgonSDK\Scripts\Paks. <ModName>.pak and <ModName.txt> are produced It also copies the output .pak file to your Chivalry 2’s Paks directory.

docs.title: Option C: Cook and package manually
docs.text:
1. Save your assets and click on File -> Cook Content for Windows to start the cooking process.
    • It may take a while to cook the entire project when cooking for the first time.
    • A large number of errors not related to your mod actor may appear in the logs. These are expected as we’re dealing with a bunch of dummy assets. It should not influence your mod actor.
    • Resulting (Cooked) assets are written to ArgonSDK\Saved\Cooked\WindowsNoEditor\TBL\Content
  2. Refer to ArgonSDK Wiki and use UnrealPak-With-Compression.bat ArgonSDK Wiki:Step 2: paking

docs.title: 6. In-Match UI (Optional)
docs.text:
You can register multiple widgets that will load together with your mod. These will be displayed in the Pause menu. The button in upper left corner toggles menu visibility.

To add a new tab widget, create a Widget Blueprint of class IngameModMenuBaseWidget and add it together with desired name to the field in #General Settings
